en: Preface to the Record of the Great Being Shan-hui,
composed by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple and National University Graduate Lou Ying:
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest the three bodies to traverse the worlds of the ten directions, propagating the six perfections to gather in those within the five realms of existence.
Sentient beings, by the very nature of sentient beings, grasp through false views and delusion; their words contradict their actions, and their dispositions run counter to principle.
Though they desire to apply themselves diligently to the profound mysteries, they merely skim the surface of the vast source. Their wisdom cannot know, and their insight cannot illuminate;

it is sufficient only to produce names and signs, becoming a veil and a fetter. Thus they encounter demons and enemies, fall under the control of external paths, and stumble headlong into the six sense-objects.
This is the realm [of the Buddha]. Within the three realms, there are none who can roll up their sleeves to challenge him, nor any who emerge as vanguard to penetrate his ranks—how tragic!
It is for this reason that the Sage expands his vast net as a teaching of great expedient means (*mahopāya*):
some were once teachers of the Benevolent One (*Śākyamuni*) and are now his disciples; some conceal the conduct of a Bodhisattva and manifest the studies of a Śrāvaka. Thus, with purity...

Taking purity as the battlefield, using the observance of precepts as defense, taking the vajra as the blade, employing skillful means as spies, taking the assembly as the generals and soldiers, and using the preaching of the Dharma as the command, he then led countless divisions to destroy the city of Māra.
All the māras within the city were completely subdued; they leaped for joy and, with great exultation, gave rise to the bodhicitta.

They are immeasurable and innumerable. Since the Nirvana at the Twin Śāla Trees, the wheel of Dharma has ceased its course and the sun of wisdom has hidden its radiance, causing the prison of the six realms of existence to grow ever more solid day by day. Therefore, we Buddhas and Bodhisattvas feel compassion for them because it is thus.
Therefore, by employing the power of his majestic spiritual authority (*vīrya*), he manifests countless bodies in order to unlock their fetters and reveal to them the essential convergence.
Thus, it is clear that the Great Being of the Twin Śāla Trees spoke of himself as being the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Maitreya;
were it not so, how could there be such spontaneous, teacherless wisdom that transcends the midst of ordinary beings, and such unhindered eloquence?

He possessed profound understanding of the scriptural treasury and constantly protected and upheld the True Dharma. He opened the eyes and ears of sentient beings who were like the deaf and blind, exactly as the sutras describe.
Vimalakīrti’s pure observance of the precepts was intended to gather in those who violated the prohibitions and cause them to return to the Right Path.

At that time, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, despite his noble status as a sovereign, applied himself with diligent devotion to the Buddha-treasure; thus, extraordinary individuals appeared together to assist him.
He assisted the Orthodox Teaching. During the time of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), among the bhikṣu-saṃgha were the wise ones:
Touduo, Huizhi, Huie, Pujian, and Pucheng. Among the lay devotees (upāsaka) were Fu Pumin, Xu Puba, Pan Puchen, and Layman Chang.

All of them practiced the six perfections and the four immeasurable minds; they purified their hearts and cleansed their conduct to adorn and uphold their bodies. They released living beings, observed a vegetarian diet, and practiced medicine.
They rescue others from suffering by extending universal compassion to all beings; they construct stupas and temples and venerate sacred images to solemnize the Buddha’s work;
they expound verses and propagate sutras and treatises to broaden their learning—all such individuals perform inconceivable deeds.
These acts serve as mutual reinforcement to transform those who are difficult to believe and difficult to edify.
He desires that they may attain the Unsurpassed Way and behold the Buddhas of the future. I, Ying, have long been obscured by the cage of afflictions;

the long night has not yet dawned. I regret that I cannot, beneath the sun and moon, personally receive his illuminating guidance. Yet I still pray that we may be reborn together in Tuṣita Heaven above and meet again at the Dragon Flower Assembly below.
Thus, like one who fells a tree and thinks of the person it sheltered, or hears the Shao music and forgets its flavor, I fear that [the fragrance of his virtue will fade].

As the dust of time scattered and dispersed, these teachings were subsequently unheard of. Thereupon, [the author] sought out the elder and compiled them into eight fascicles, forming this biography to be shown to future generations. Thus it is said.
Record of the Great Being Shan-hui, Scroll One.
The Great Being’s surname was Fu, his given name was Xi, and his courtesy name was Hsüan-feng. He was a native of K’i-ting Village in Wu-shang County, Tung-yang Prefecture.
Wu-shang is the present-day Yi-wu County. His father’s name was Hsüan-tz’u, with the courtesy name Kuang-ai; his mother was of the Wang clan. For generations, they had been farmers.
He was born on the eighth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, the Dingchou year. He was upright, serene, pure, and harmonious, possessing no attachments.
In his youth, he did not pursue formal studies; at times he would fish with the villagers, and whenever he caught a fish, he would always place it in a bamboo basket.

He submerged himself in deep water and made this vow: "Those who wish to go, may they go; those who wish to stay, may they stay. At that time, people considered him a fool. Pujian, Pucheng. In the first year of the Putong era, at the age of twenty-four, he was fishing upstream at the foot of Jiting Pond when he encountered a foreign monk named Sōngtóuduó (Śramaṇa Śāṇavāsa).
The monk said to the Great Being, "In the past, I and you made a vow before Vipaśyin Buddha to deliver sentient beings.
You now possess all the enjoyments within the Tuṣita Heaven; when will you [fulfill this vow]?"
When they were about to return, the Great Being merely stared with wide-open eyes. The dhūta practitioner said, "Try looking at your reflection in the water.
The Great Being followed this advice and saw his own circular halo and jeweled crown; he then realized his former causes and said, "In the place of the smelting furnace, there is much dull iron."

"Under the gate of a skilled physician, there are many patients; one must take the salvation of sentient beings as the urgent priority. What leisure is there to contemplate the pleasures of the celestial palaces?
Thereupon, he cast aside his fishing gear and, taking his companion with him, returned home. He then asked for a place to cultivate the Way.
The Dhūta pointed to two *śāla* trees beneath a pine mountain and said, "This will suffice. This is the present-day Shuanglin Temple. The Mahāsattva established [his practice] here.
The Hermit styled himself the "Future Bodhisattva of Liberation and Great Wisdom Beneath the Twin Sala Trees. He cultivated fruits and vegetables and worked as a hired laborer for others.
Together with his wife, Miaoguang, he would work by day and return home at night to expound the Buddha-dharma.

After seven years of ascetic practice, one day, while sitting in meditative seclusion, he beheld the three Buddhas—Śākyamuni, Suvarṇapuṣpa, and Dīpaṃkara—approaching from the east, emitting light like...

One day, he again saw a golden light descend from heaven and gather upon the Great Being’s body. From this body, a wondrous fragrance constantly issued forth. He frequently heard a voice chanting from the air:
"On the day you attain enlightenment, you shall succeed Śākyamuni in sitting at the site of awakening.

Subsequently, the fourfold assembly gathered there regularly to inquire after his well-being and pay their respects. The regional governor, Wang Xiu, deemed this to be sorcery and delusion, and imprisoned him for several weeks. The Great...

The scholar abstained from food and drink, which caused the multitude to marvel at him all the more; they subsequently released him. The Great Being returned to the mountains and applied himself with even greater diligence.
Those who wished to serve him as their teacher from near and far increased daily. Every morning when the bell rang, an immortal would descend through the air.
He followed and rejoiced in their practice of the Way. He once said to his disciples, "I have attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi," and he also said, "I have attained untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna).
His disciples all remarked, "The Śūraṅgama Samādhi can only be attained by Bodhisattvas dwelling in the tenth stage (bhūmi).
Therefore, we know that this Great Being is a Bodhisattva dwelling in the tenth stage who merely manifests traces in accordance with ordinary people. The Great Being desired—

In the chapter on "Guiding the Multitudes," he first transformed his wife and children, causing them to resolve upon the Way. They immediately abandoned their fields and houses, invited the fourfold assembly, and established a great assembly, whereupon he spoke these verses:
He cast aside his private concerns to manifest a heavenly mind and exhausted his resources to establish this assembly for the good.
May he vow to deliver all sentient beings until they all soar beyond the three realms; may he take refuge in the Unsurpassed One and look up with gratitude so that all may be sheltered.
In that year of famine, after the assembly was established, not even a peck of grain remained in any household. Among the neighbors were Fu Fang and Fu Ziliang, and others.
He entered the mountains to make offerings. The Great Being exhorted his wife and children to sell themselves to support the assembly.
Miaoguang received their command and said, "I only wish that all sentient beings may, by this means, attain liberation together.

In the third month of the second year of the Datong era, Fu Zhongchang and Fu Sengju of the same village purchased him for fifty thousand coins. Having obtained the money, the Great Being immediately prepared the provisions.

At the great assembly, he made this vow: "I, the disciple Shanhui, prostrate before the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, and the eternally abiding Triple Gem throughout the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm.

I now relinquish my wife and children to universally eliminate calamities and accumulate merit for all sentient beings in the miserable realms of the three worlds, to extinguish their defilements and sins, and that they may together realize Bodhi. More than a month later...
The Fu family sent Miaoguang and the others back to the mountain. The Great Being (Dashi) had a servant who had run away and hidden to become a thief.

At that time, two neighbors, Fu Fang and Fu Yang, exhausted their entire property to offer it as alms. The Great Being then used these funds to organize a "Sacrificial Retreat for the Suffering" on behalf of the missing servant, lasting for seven weeks of seven days each.
Miaoguang spun thread and worked for hire, never resting even for a moment. Fu Fang also pawned his wife and children to obtain further funds.
He offered rice as an offering, which the Mahāsattva then distributed further to various practitioners of the Way. Thereafter, his spiritual manifestations increased even more.

Some people slandered and reviled him, yet the Mahāsattva felt only redoubled compassion for them. One day, he went to his uncle’s house and declared, "I am Maitreya; I have come specifically to transform you.
You, my uncle, should pay me homage. His uncle then prostrated himself. He then wished to go to see his great-uncle, Master Fu.

Fu initially did not believe him. Miaoguang admonished him, saying, "He claims you have lost your mind; how could there be any propriety in you, his great-uncle, performing a prostration? Be careful not to go.
The Great Being (Bodhisattva) immediately brushed his chest, which turned golden in color and emitted a celestial fragrance, showing it to Miaoguang.
Miaoguang still said, "Do not go. The Great Being nevertheless went to Fu’s location and told him to perform a prostration. Fu remained firm and would not.

When [Hui]fu returned from following the Great Being, Miaoguang asked, "Did you pay homage? He replied, "Although I have not yet paid homage today, tomorrow I shall certainly pay homage at every step.
That night, Fu dreamed that eight men escorted the Great Being away; Fu followed them and questioned them.
A person scolded him, saying, "You are arrogant and do not follow the holy instructions; what more do you ask now?
Suddenly, he saw the Great Being (Mahāsattva), his golden form extraordinary, soaring through the air as he walked. Daofu pursued him, but saw only a stone wall stretching across the sky;

the Great Being and his attendants passed straight through it without obstruction. Daofu could not proceed further. Upon waking, he was filled with sorrow and regret. At dawn, he entered the mountains and gradually began to perceive a wondrous fragrance.
Seeing the Great Being from afar, he shed tears and prostrated himself, vowing to become his disciple. The Great Being said, "I have descended from Tuṣita precisely to receive you.
Master Fu then took him as his preceptor, and his three karmas became pure. At that time, the śramaṇa Huìjí came to the Twin Trees;
the Great Being expounded for him the Unsurpassed Bodhi, and Huìjí vowed to become his disciple.
First: The Great Being (Mahāsattva) experienced a dream in which a five-colored circular light emerged from the left side of his neck;

his body ascended into the void and descended to the summit of the mountain where he resided, specifically on its southeastern face. Upon waking, Huìjí arrived, and the Great Being remained on this mountain.

Thereafter, as Huìjí traveled everywhere to teach and transform others, he constantly declared that the Great Being was an emanation-body (nirmāṇakāya) of Maitreya. Whenever the Great Being preached or...
While performing meritorious deeds, he requested the Buddha to withdraw his radiance. His two eyes constantly emitted golden light, and he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"If one who studies the Way does not encounter a teacher of non-arising (*anutpāda*), they will ultimately not attain the Way. I am one who has realized non-arising before my very eyes.
Previously I concealed this matter; now I shall no longer hide it, so as to reveal it to you. Furthermore, when a disciple prostrated, the Mahāsattva said because of it:
He said to him, "Do not prostrate to me; rather, prostrate to the Buddha within the hall, for that is my own image.

He further said, "In a dream, I recalled my teacher of the past, named the World-Honored One Shanming (Good Enlightenment). Someone asked, "Was the World-Honored One Shanming your teacher when you attained the Way, or was he your teacher when you first resolved to attain enlightenment?
He replied, "He was not my teacher when I first resolved to attain enlightenment. That Buddha appeared..."
In a past age, I was a king and made offerings to that Buddha. That Buddha’s lifespan was eighty thousand years;
when I become a Buddha, my lifespan shall likewise be so. In a dream, I obtained the name of a teacher; remembering his compassionate appearance, I wept tears all night long.
Again, he said: "In a dream, I saw Śākyamuni extend his palm to join with my hand. [The questioner] asked: "What kind of omen is this? [He] replied: "This..."
"This is merely my mind resonating with the mind of the World-Honored One.
In the third year of the Zhongda Tong era, the Great Being and his disciples were about ten *li* east of their residence on Mount Yunhuang.

He excavated the site to establish a vihāra and planted hemp, beans, taro, vegetables, and the like. When the autumn harvest arrived, a man named Jia Tanying from Cishouli suddenly came to dispute the land.
The Mahāsattva immediately gave it to him. The Mahāsattva resided at both Songshan and Yunhuang;
the forested foothills were lush and verdant, yet many fierce beasts inhabited them, such that people were constantly afraid of them. The Mahāsattva, however, always...
He fed him with leftover food, whereupon [the snake] hid itself away from that time forward.
In the sixth year of the Datong era, the Great Being said, "The secluded location of the Twin Trees does not allow for the broad conversion of sentient beings;
I wish to go to the imperial court to see the Son of Heaven and proclaim the True Teaching. On the eighteenth day of the first month, he dispatched his disciple Fu Yang to present [a memorial].
Written to Emperor Wu of the Liang Dynasty: The Mahāsattva of Future Liberation, Śubhavyūha, beneath the twin śāla trees, addresses the Sovereign, the World-Saving Bodhisattva:
"The Mahāsattva now wishes to set forth the superior, middling, and inferior forms of goodness; I hope you will be able to receive and uphold them. As for the superior goodness:
taking an empty mind as its foundation, non-attachment as its principle, formlessness as its cause, and nirvāṇa as its fruit. As for the middling..."
Excellent. To govern oneself is the foundation; to govern the state is the primary principle. Thus, in both the heavens and the human realm, the retribution is peace and happiness.
Furthermore, it is excellent to protect and nourish all sentient beings, to overcome cruelty and eliminate killing, and to cause all the common people to universally observe the six fast days.

Now, this Great Being has established a vow to propagate the orthodox teaching and universally deliver all living beings; therefore, he has dispatched his disciple Huǎng to submit this notification. Huǎng respectfully [reports].

The letter reached the capital. [Hui]yǎng went to see He Chāng, the Director of the Court of Music. Upon seeing the letter, Chāng raised an objection, saying, "Even the National Preceptor Zhìzě still submits formal petitions;
how much more so for a Great Being and a subject of the state to suddenly compose a plain letter? How could I dare present it?

Huiyǎng said, "I have come from the East recently, fearing that no one would deliver this letter for me. Therefore, I have made a vow in my heart and burned my hand by the side of the imperial road, hoping that—"
The Emperor heard this. Upon hearing these words, Chang took the letter to Tongtai Temple to see Dharma Master Hao, and they discussed together how to present it as a memorial to the throne.
An imperial decree was issued for him to attend court. The Great Being arrived at Jiangshan on the nineteenth day of the twelfth month, and reached the capital at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.
on the eighth day of the intercalary twelfth month. Previously, when Emperor Wu had heard of the Great Being’s spiritual wonders, he immediately...
The Emperor ordered the gatekeepers to lock all the doors in advance. The Great Being had already known this in his mind beforehand; he had prepared a pair of large wooden mallets.

He first struck one door, and all the doors opened simultaneously. He entered directly into the Hall of Good Words (Shanyan Dian) and, refusing to prostrate himself as required, went straight up onto the precious couch presented by the Western Kingdom.
This couch was one that had been obtained by Prince Zhaoming, the Dharma Master Zhizhe, and the Great Being.
He sat down to listen. The Emperor asked the Great Being, "Whom do you serve as your teacher? He replied, "I follow from nowhere; I have no teacher to serve, and I serve nothing.
When the meal was finished, he returned to Zhongshan Dinglin Temple. By imperial decree, he was provided with all necessary provisions.
From then on, famous monks gathered there like clouds, and the place was constantly graced by the descent of sweet dew.
In the first month of the first year of the Dàtóng era, the Emperor visited the Chóngyún Hall in Huálín Garden and invited the fourfold assembly of monks and nuns.
He personally lectured on the *Triprajñā-pāramitā Sūtra*. At that time, high officials sat in continuous rows, and the seats were filled with those wearing the *diǎo* and *fú* ribbons.

By imperial decree, a separate couch was specially prepared for the Great Being (the Master), who was attended by four courtiers. At that moment, Liú Zhōngjí arrived and asked the Great Being why he did not [participate in the lecture].

The subject addressed the Son of Heaven: "I am not a friend to the feudal lords. The Great Master replied: "In reverence there is no nature of reverence; in non-reverence there is no mind of non-reverence.
When the assembly had gathered, the Emperor ascended the throne, yet the Great Master alone did not rise. The Emperor repeatedly asked him the reason for this.

The Great Being replied, "If the ground of the Dharma were to move, all phenomena would be unsettled. At that time, the kings and dukes presented offerings and requested the assembly to recite the sutras;
however, the Great Being remained silent. When people asked him the reason for this, he replied, "Both speech and silence are Buddha-activities.
The Crown Prince sent someone to inquire, "Why do you not engage in discussion? He replied, "One should know that what is spoken is neither long nor [short]."
It is neither short nor long, neither broad nor narrow, neither finite nor infinite; it is suchness, the true principle. What more need be said?
When the assembly had dispersed, the Emperor presented the Bodhisattva with two jewels—one of water and one of fire—each exceeding an inch in diameter, perfectly round, brilliant, and translucent.
Since the Bodhisattva dwelt in the mountains, water and fire were difficult to obtain; therefore, the Emperor bestowed these jewels upon him so that he might constantly draw water and fire from them.
Regarding the sun and moon: at one time, a king and several high officials went to the Great Being’s dwelling and saw that he was sitting improperly.
They asked, "Why do you not sit upright? He replied, "An upright person has no fixed nature of uprightness; a slanted person has no fixed mind of slant.
One day, the Emperor invited him to the Shouguang Hall to preach the Dharma, and it was not until nightfall that he departed.
In the fourth month, he returned once more to Mount Yunhuang. On the second day of the ninth month, he again dispatched Fu Yang to present a letter to the Emperor, saying:
"The Great Being of Good Wisdom, who shall attain liberation beneath the twin śāla trees, addresses the Sovereign, the Bodhisattva Savior of the World."
"Now there is a wish-fulfilling jewel, pure and liberated, illuminating the ten directions; its radiance and color are subtle and wondrous, beyond the reach of thought.
I wish to bestow it upon the Lord of Men; if you can accept it, you shall swiftly attain Bodhi. The Emperor issued an edict, saying:
"If you wish to look after me, that would be most excellent."
In the fifth year of the Datong era, he began his journey back to the capital. Upon reaching Mount Zhong, he addressed the Emperor with this report:
"Does Your Majesty possess a mind that seeks to distinguish? Does the Great Being possess a doctrine that seeks to debate? The Emperor replied:
"Whether there is a mind or no mind, both enter into the reality-limit (*bhūtatathatā*). The reality-limit transcends verbal expression; therein is neither distinction nor debate."
On the sixteenth day of the third month, the Emperor discussed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) with the Great Being (Bodhisattva) in the Shouguang Hall.
The Great Being said, "It is stilled, yet not extinguished. The Emperor said, "If it is stilled yet not extinguished, then it possesses form;

therefore, it is dull. The Great Being said, "All dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent. The Emperor said, "I respectfully accept this instruction. The Great Being said, "Of all forms and appearances, there are none that do not..."
Returning to emptiness: the hundred rivers do not exceed the great ocean; the myriad dharmas do not go beyond True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Among the three realms and ninety-six paths, the Tathāgata alone transcends them all as the supreme. He regards all sentient beings universally as his own self, as if they were his own infants.

In the world, nothing is peaceful that is not in accord with the Way (*dharma*); nothing is joyful that is not in accord with principle (*li*). The Emperor remained silent. The Great Being withdrew. This concludes the tenth [section].
On the eighth day, the Great Being composed a verse and presented it to the Emperor as a response to the meaning of "cessation without extinction. The words said:
"If there were cessation and extinction, One would see suffering and sever the origin; If one were thus proceeding toward nirvāṇa, Then there would be a sense of 'mine' and no equality.
One would not encounter great compassion; Since there would be no great compassion, There would still be negligence."
Practicing the study of non-abiding, one does not head toward nirvāṇa. If one were to head toward nirvāṇa, it would constitute an obstruction for the Siddhārtha who possesses marks;
it would cause him to head toward nirvāṇa, which is cessation without extinction. It is merely the cessation of攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective conditions) without the cessation of the original non-being.
Since original non-being is unarisen, it is now not extinguished; thus, one does not head toward nirvāṇa.
Not being attached to the world is called great compassion; it is the absence of "mine," as well as the absence of "self" and "other.
Pervading all forms while lacking the nature of form is called non-negligence.
Why not treat all sentient beings with non-negligence—regarding them as one's own infants, regarding them as one's own self, and always desiring their benefit and peace?
How can one abide thus? There is no existence in the past, no existence in the present, and no existence in the future;
the three periods of time are pure. One benefits all beings, bringing about their collective liberation.
Furthermore, one contemplates how the Single Vehicle enters all vehicles, and how all vehicles return to enter the Single Vehicle. Moreover, one contemplates the practice of cultivation.
*The Chapter on Immeasurable Paths*: Universally saving all sentient beings, yet without grasping at a self;
neither bound nor liberated, continuing until the end of the future—this is what is called "diligence.

In the sixth year of the Datong era, he took leave of the Emperor and returned to the East. Several months later, for the sake of meritorious works, he returned once more to the capital and stayed there.
At Mount Jiangshan, [Huiyuan] dispatched Fu Yang to present a letter to the Emperor, saying:

"The Great Being of Future Liberation and Good Wisdom beneath the twin śāla trees addresses the National Lord, the World-Saving Bodhisattva. Your Majesty’s nature accords with the Right Path, and you tread upon Suchness (*tathatā*).
The Great Being descends for the sake of *bodhi* and thus appears humble; Your Majesty ascends for the sake of *bodhi* and thus appears exalted. Through the resonance of these karmic conditions..."
It is so; thus the work of attaining Buddhahood is accomplished. Now, I have come specifically to universally exhort all to together cultivate the True Path.
This is respectfully submitted. At that time, He Chang was acting as an external envoy; this letter had not yet reached him. Then, a śramaṇa asked, saying: "Great Being, is today a great day?"
"Is it that the future day is great? He replied, "It may be that today is small and the future day is great; it may also be that today is great and the future day is small. Why is this?

For one cultivates the Path while on the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), yet practices the causes for the fruit while on the stage of fruition. One constantly acts without anything being trodden upon."
He constantly delivered those who were not yet saved. At that time, he petitioned the Emperor to establish a monastery between two *śāla* trees, naming it "Double Forest" (*Śālavana*).

Prior to the monastery’s construction, these two trees had grown from separate roots, yet their branches and leaves were joined together; auspicious vapors issued from the hollows of the wood, and above them, a pair of cranes nested and soared, calling out in harmony.
When the Great Master returned to construct the Buddha hall, there was already a white poplar tree standing before the hall.
Its branches and leaves were exceptionally beautiful and extraordinary. Whenever he walked beneath it, he would constantly hear celestial music and receive the descent of sweet nectar (*amṛta*).

The Great Being ordered this tree to be cut down for an image in the palace. Before long, a master woodworker arrived of his own accord. Furthermore, at the site of the tree, he constructed a nine-story brick stupa, which remains to this day.
He personally transcribed over one thousand scrolls of sutras and vinaya texts. He addressed the Buddha, making a vow that all sentient beings might be freed from suffering.
For the sake of liberation, the Great Being came to the capital three times; those he converted, both monastics and laity, were beyond counting.
In the seventh year of the Datong era, he said to his disciples, "Among the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, I am but one Buddha.
If you wish to be born among the thousand Buddhas, you shall immediately behold me. A disciple asked, "If there is another person with deep karmic obstructions, Great Being..."
"Did you know this beforehand? They replied, "Could there be anything that a Bodhisattva in his final birth does not know?
When I was about to sit at the site of enlightenment, this person was a messenger of Māra who created obstacles for me; I intended to use this very situation as a Dharma-gate.
You all should simply observe how I encountered such affliction and turmoil yet did not give rise to anger. Why is it that you, when faced with such minor hindrances..."
"I wish to divide heaven and separate earth; yet I deliver all beings with equal impartiality, without distinction.

He spoke again, saying, "I am a messenger of the Tathāgata, come from the midst of Suchness (tathatā). His disciple asked, "Since you, Master, are thus, why do you not possess the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā)?
He replied, "Even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess the six supernormal powers. You should observe that the causal origination of my own conduct and practice is such as this."
"How could I lack the six supernormal powers? For now, I merely manifest in accordance with ordinary beings. One day, he addressed the assembly again, saying:
"When I cast off this body, my period of sojourn shall be such that I will briefly pass through the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven before returning to the Tuṣita Heaven.
If you wish to be born there, you will immediately be able to see me."
In the eighth year of the Dàtóng era, he established a vow to observe the Upper Fast (shàngzhāi) and composed a prayer, saying: "I, the disciple Shànhuì, now address Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One;
the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; and the eternally abiding Triple Gem that pervades all of space and the entire dharma-realm."
The disciple reflected to himself: "In this life, I have had nothing to offer as a gift from my own heart to rescue suffering sentient beings.
From this day forth, I take a vow to observe the supreme fast for three years, abstaining from food and drink on every sixth day of the month. Through the hardship of this hunger and thirst,"
On behalf of all sentient beings, may they repay their karmic debts, shorten the kalpas of suffering, and swiftly attain liberation.
With food that requires no consumption, may they perform extensive acts of giving. May all sentient beings, in every lifetime, be fully provided with immeasurable wealth and Dharma;
may they forever be free from the defilement of craving, refrain from the three types of karma, attain the Great Dhāraṇī, subdue all māras, and realize the Unsurpassed Way.
In the tenth year of the Dàtóng era, the Great Being entrusted the Buddha images and sūtras to the assembly of virtuous practitioners.
Furthermore, he relinquished all his dwellings, fields, and household goods to establish a vihāra and convene a great dharma assembly.

He made this formal declaration before the Buddhas for the sake of all beings throughout the ten directions and three periods of time—those of the six destinies and four modes of birth—treating enemies and kin with equal impartiality, and making offerings to the Triple Gem.

All assemblies shall perform the work of a Buddha. All sentient beings throughout the boundless lands of the ten directions in this world, if they commit any physical, verbal, or mental karma that creates all manner of immeasurable sins, will because of these fall into the great hells.
Furthermore, due to the retribution of their karma, they may be born as animals and undergo manifold sufferings;

or they may be born among humans, impoverished and lowly, blind, deaf, mute, or otherwise lacking in sensory faculties. Or they may be bound in shackles and fetters, exiled, or confined in prisons, enduring immeasurable hardships and calamities.
Or they may fail to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, or behold the Sangha; failing to encounter spiritual friends, they lack the cause for liberation.
With these offerings, he looked up and entreated the World-Honored One: "May Your compassionate power extinguish [my suffering] so that I may swiftly attain liberation;

may I meet with virtuous friends, hear the Dharma, realize the Way, and give rise to the bodhicitta. Having exhausted all his resources as a great man—his wealth and house—he was left without a place to shelter his body.
He then established a grass hut, and Miaoguang likewise established a hut for herself. Wearing clothes of grass and eating from the woods, they applied themselves diligently day and night.

It was a time of suffering. Having only just obtained a small measure of sufficiency, suddenly a band of robbers arrived. They threatened him with blades, yet the Great Being showed no sign of fear from the outset.
He spoke to them calmly, saying, "If you require wealth and goods, take as much as you wish. Why are you so angry? When the robbers had departed, the house was empty;
however, there were still more than two hundred hu of rice remaining. He then thought to himself: "It is because of having a body that all these people come into being."
For those with sinful karma, after their lives end, they will inevitably fall into hell and suffer great misery for a long time.

Consequently, he gave up a hundred *hu* of rice to provide a feast offering to the Triple Gem for the sake of repenting his evil deeds. The small pond in front of his house had coincidentally run dry;
the Great Being took all the insects and fish and cast them into the great river. Those that died were buried at the foot of the mountain, along with the oxen and dogs.

He also buried those who had died. Deeply contemplating how such beings wander through the miserable realms of saṃsāra with no prospect of liberation, he further donated two hundred *hu* of rice to establish a feast for fish, dogs, and others, making offerings to the Triple Gem. Admiring this noble example, he then composed a verse:
In the past, the Sages gave up their heads and eyes; the Prince saved the tiger’s life.
The Compassionate One abandoned his kingdom to practice patience, uprooting both enemies and kin. Now that I have heard of these virtues, I look up with longing for the causes of Bodhi.
I shall give all my resources to deliver oxen and dogs, and sacrifice my life to save the bodies of fish. May we be companions forever in eternal bliss.
Together we shall proceed to the ford of Nirvāṇa; alike we shall meet where the mundane and the non-mundane are one; equally we shall realize where the true and the non-true are identical.
In the second month of the second year of Taicheng, the Great Being again relinquished his fields, gardens, and property, and on the fifteenth day, he established a dharma assembly.
For the sake of this land, throughout the ten directions and all Buddha-worlds, may those in the six realms and four modes of birth regard enemies and kin with equal impartiality.
May they make offerings to the Triple Gem, and as the Buddhas abide in the world, universally deliver all living beings. Then he spoke in verse:
Dedicating all resources for the sake of goodness, I take refuge in the God among Gods. I look up and entreat you to suspend your radiance and let your grace flow throughout the great trichiliocosm.
May those in the three miserable realms all attain liberation, and may those in the six destinies transcend the mundane to reach the supramundane.
In the universal assembly, realize both existence and non-existence; together, realize both conditions and the unconditioned.
Furthermore, a verse says:
Secluded on the cliffs, I have cultivated the True Path, Resting here for more than thirty years. Far removed from my forest-dwelling friends, I take refuge in the profound void of the Emperor.
I shall convene an assembly to proclaim the sutras and perform repentance, In order to sweep away the dust and ruins of that realm.
May all those in the impure realms of no leisure have minds as pure as lotuses; may they together realize the principle of the three emptinesses and equally attain the Suchness of the Great Being.
Furthermore, desiring to observe the supreme fast of not eating and to offer one's body as a lamp, one universally makes offerings for the sake of all beings.
On the fifteenth day of the third month, he addressed the assembly, saying:

"In the past, I heard that the Great Being Candraprabha gave away his head in extensive charity, and Prince Viśvantara saved the destitute and relieved the needy, never begrudging his life or wealth. As clarified in the sutras, such a person will before long attain Buddhahood.
Therefore, I, though of humble and insignificant station, look up to these holy examples and have resolved my heart to vow to give away my body, life, and wealth universally."
To make offerings to all Buddhas, he strictly observed the supreme fast of non-eating and attained parinirvāṇa.
With resolute intent, he burned his body as a great bright lamp to make offerings to the Triple Gem. Now, on the eighth day of the coming month, he first addressed the assembly, saying:
"Do not harbor grief or distress. All things have birth and death; all affairs have success and failure. Under heaven..."
All who are bound by affection must inevitably part. Now, casting off this defiled and turbid body, I shall attain the birthless, pure Dharma-body.
I pray only that you, my followers, harbor no sorrowful attachment; may we never be parted throughout life after life, remaining as kinsmen until the attainment of the Buddha-way.
Let us simply lead one another to prepare firewood together and perform our final rites upon the summit of the Śāla Grove mountain.

The Fire Shrine. By virtue of these causes and conditions, may they necessarily perform the work of a Buddha in future worlds, universally delivering all beings so that they may together attain liberation.

On the eighth day of the fourth month, nineteen disciples, including Liu Jianyi and Fan Nantu, each requested to act as representatives for their master, observing the supreme fast of non-eating and offering the sacrifice of self-immolation to the Triple Gem. Furthermore—
The disciple Zhu Jiangu burned one finger as a lamp. Chen Chao sold himself;
Yao Puxun, Zhi Lang, and others took up employment, each using their earnings to make offerings to their masters.

They universally vowed that all beings, through successive births and rebirths, would always encounter the Buddhas, hear the Dharma and awaken to the Way, and together realize non-arising. On the ninth day of this month, the disciple Liu He...
Mu and Zhou Jiangu both burned off a finger as a lamp. Their disciple Lou Baoyin pierced his heart.
Ge Xuangao cut off both his left and right ears. The bhikṣu Bodhi and the upāsikā Luo Miaode both cut off their left ears.
The bhikṣus Zhilang, Zhipin, and twenty-two others cut off their right ears. They made this vow: "Disciple Bodhi..."

[And so forth. We respectfully address Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One; all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; and the eternally abiding Triple Gem throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasive Dharma-realm.

We humbly beseech our Master: having vowed to propagate the holy teachings and universally deliver all sentient beings, you have renounced body, life, and wealth, even burning your own body as a lamp, universally making offerings to all Buddhas on behalf of all beings.
We now solemnly sever our ears and pierce our hearts, using the blood to sprinkle the ground.

On behalf of our teacher and master, we universally offer worship to all Buddhas. We have humbly heard that the Great Awakened One, the Compassionate Father, takes pity upon and nurtures all living beings;
moved by grief for the lives of creatures, he cultivated the practice of Great Compassion to rescue and deliver all conscious beings. This has continued through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.

As he approached the proclamation of *nirvāṇa*, the devas entreated him, whereupon he stayed his departure for as long as the sands of the Ganges. Both ordinary beings and sages rejoiced in this. Therefore, we, [the undersigned], having humbly observed...

The Master, together with about twenty members of the monastic community, was about to adorn the Buddha-field, cause the sound of the Dharma to thunder forth, and beat the drum of fearlessness to extensively benefit the boundless.
Having disciplined himself and cast away his body, he accomplished supreme virtue; this is truly an inconceivable superior practice, a realm beyond that of ordinary beings.
We, however, have not yet been able to shed our transgressions or cast off our faults; our karmic defilements are deep and heavy. Now...
I respectfully offer my ears and burn my fingers, earnestly entreating you with the utmost sincerity. It is like a destitute child wandering alone, having lost his father;

how much more so for one who has lost its mother while still in the womb—then it falls blindly into a dark abyss, where the sun of wisdom is forever obscured. The Semblance Dharma will then collapse, and the light of insight will vanish.

Sentient beings are in turmoil, drowning in the river of craving. How painful and tragic! We prostrate ourselves with the earnest wish that you, our Master, will restrain your majestic power and remain stationary, staying long in this world.
May you look upon all living beings with compassion, extending mercy to those in the six realms; may you care for the orphaned and the destitute, bringing benefit and peace to the poor and the aged.

May all deluded followers be universally enlightened, equally attaining non-arising and together returning to quiescent extinction. We humbly pray that Your Great Compassion will deign to grant this request.

Furthermore, there were fifteen bhikṣuṇīs, including Fatao and Fajian, who each observed the three-day fast without food, requesting that the Master remain for a long time to propagate the True Teaching. Additionally, there was the bhikṣu Pujie, who resided...
Shi Fu Chang, Fu Yuan, and forty-two others prostrated themselves and paid homage at the feet of the Great Being.

They humbly heard that when the Sun of the Buddha first shone its light, he contemplated for twenty-one days whether, because the faculties of sentient beings were dull and they were blinded by attachment to pleasure and ignorance, he should not preach the Dharma but instead enter Nirvana swiftly.
Thereupon, Śakra and Brahmā entreated him, and he immediately turned the Wheel of Dharma. Throughout those years, he constantly...
He poured down the rain of the Dharma, benefiting immeasurable beings. He concealed his radiance beneath the eight trees and entrusted the Dharma to the four reliances.

Our Master, in accord with his original vows, rose up transcendentally; sitting upright at the twin śāla trees, he did not shrink from toil or suffering, desiring to widely propagate the Buddha-Dharma and circulate the True Path.
How can you now wish to set a date for his cremation? It is like an infant losing its mother—this is no mere metaphor. He was a ship upon the ocean...
The [teachings] have been destroyed and lost; they are no longer a source of suffering. The Original Teacher, the Eye of the World, has already passed away with his moon of wisdom waning.

The Compassionate Guide, the Sun of Wisdom, has not yet shone. In these present long nights, there is a pressing need for illumination. We, Ji and the others, have resolved our wills so deeply that we would sprinkle our blood upon the ground.
I specifically beg you to take heed until the end of your life in Jambudvīpa.
In the third year of the Taicheng era, as the destiny of the Liang dynasty was nearing its end, calamities arose one after another.

When disaster struck the Great Being’s native village, he distributed all his wealth and possessions to the hungry and the poor. He exhorted his disciples to gather wild herbs together to cook porridge, and everyone shared their portions to eat.
He used these means to provide relief for the local villages.
In the first and second years of the Dàbǎo era, the Great Master again exhorted his disciples to cook gruel, following the established practices of the Tàiqīng era.
In the spring of that year, there were no plow oxen in the village; the Great Master therefore sent his disciples to personally plant the crops, bringing oxen to assist the people.
He cultivated his fields only to the extent necessary for his own needs, tilling no more than half a *mu* of his own land.

On the sixteenth day of the first month in the first year of the Chengsheng era, the Great Being further relinquished his fields, gardens, household property, oxen, calves, granaries, and treasuries to sponsor a Dharma assembly.
From that time forth, every year on the tenth day of the first month, he would relinquish two thousand *hu* of rice to sponsor the assembly.
At the Dharma assembly, he spoke in verse:
"I exhaust my resources for the sake of all beings, To offer worship to the God among Gods.

I look up and pray that the rain of nectar may flow forth, Universally and boundlessly, so that all within the six realms May receive its nourishment, and likewise those in the four miserable destinies."
The universal assembly is truly neither real nor unreal; together they realize the firm and the non-firm.
On the twentieth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Shaotai era, the Great Being addressed the assembly, saying:

"I have heard that since time immemorial, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One has sacrificed his head, eyes, and treasures to benefit and bring peace to the six realms of existence. Furthermore, I have heard the sutras state that the Buddha-dharma is about to..."
At the time of destruction, various calamities will first gather like clouds; the people will suffer in misery, and many will die.

Next, there will be a water disaster, just as we see now, which shall arrive in due course. Who can, for the sake of all sentient beings, disregard their own body and life, further observe the supreme fast of non-eating, and burn their bodies to attain extinction?
Using this lamp of a body, they shall universally make offerings to the Three [Jewels] on behalf of all.
The Jewel [requested that] the Buddha remain in the world to universally deliver all sentient beings.

On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month, his disciple Fan Nantuo, having observed the superior fast (upavāsa), performed the rite of self-immolation at the summit of Mount Shuanglin and attained parinirvāṇa.
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, the bhikṣu Fakuang performed the rite of self-immolation at the foot of Mount Tiantai in Shifeng County and attained parinirvāṇa. The first year of Taiping.
On the first day of the third month of that year, the upāsikā’s son Yan subsequently entered fire at the summit of Mount Shuanglin to attain parinirvāṇa.
On the eighteenth day of the second month of the first year of the Yongding era of the Chen dynasty, the Mahāsattva addressed the assembly, saying: "Now, the world is beset by many calamities."

The suffering of the people became extreme. Who could perform such asceticism as to burn their fingers as an offering, universally making offerings to the Triple Gem on behalf of all, entreating the Buddha to remain in the world to universally deliver all living beings? At that time, there were three bhikṣus: Huǐhǎi, Pútí, and Fǎjiě.
The laymen Pucheng and seven others respectfully accepted the command. The bhikṣu Faru and the layman Bao Yue—these two—hooked their bodies to suspend the lamps.
The Great Being spoke again: "Who can cut off their own ears to shed blood, mix incense with it, and sprinkle it upon the ground as an offering for the sake of all to the Triple Gem?
At that time, there were twelve individuals, including the bhikṣu Zhiyun and others, as well as the śrāmaṇeras Hui... [text fragment].

There were ten people in total, including Pudu (Universal Equality), Puzhi (Universal Knowledge), Huiju (Wisdom Torch), and others—twenty-three people in all—and seventeen people including Xia'er Shanjue (Child Good Awakening) and others, totaling sixty-two people.
They respectfully received the command to cut off their ears and draw blood, which they mixed with incense and sprinkled upon the ground.
The Great Being spoke again: "Who is able to observe the 'upper fast' of not eating and entreat the Buddha to remain in the world?
At that time, there were twenty-six bhikṣus, including Tánzhǎn; nine śrāmaṇerīs, including Huìjiān; and the children Fǎjí and Miàozhēn.

The upāsikā Píngděng, Fǎtiàn, and others—ten people in total—and the Daoist practitioners Chén Lìngchéng, Xú Yǐn, and others—a total of forty-nine people—vowed to observe the supreme fast of non-eating.
The Mahāsattva said to the assembly, "My companions for the shared deliverance of sentient beings are nearly exhausted;
only Pán and Xú have not yet revealed their names. Among them was the disciple Fù Pǔmǐn.
This was Mañjuśrī. The śramaṇa Huìhé was my disciple who understands the meaning; he too was a sage, yet his rank in practice was not high.
The Venerable Huìjí was Avalokiteśvara, acting as my disciple. As for Layman Chāng, he was Ānanda.
While living in the world, Chāng’s appearance and conduct appeared dull and inferior, such that people could not help but slight him. Thus...
He admonished his disciples, saying: "None of you should look down upon the layman Chang. His passing was extremely easy, without any lingering pain or distress;
his complexion was bright and clear, even more radiant than usual. Only after he had passed away did the Great Being say, 'This was indeed Ānanda.
Once, a śramaṇa came to visit the Great Being and said: 'I have heard that the Great Being practices the bodhisattva path. A bodhisattva..."
Such a person would give their head for one who asks for a head, and their eyes for one who asks for eyes; they would not begrudge even their kingdom, city, wife, or children.
Now, this Great Being is asked for the incense burner in his hand. If he gives it, he is truly a Bodhisattva; if he does not, he is not.
The Great Being said, "Whether I relinquish it or do not relinquish it, neither is [the true] Bodhisattva. The śramaṇa forcibly took it away himself. After about ten days had passed, [he returned].
Someone came and asked, "Previously, there was someone who forcibly seized this incense burner. What do you think of this? The Great Being replied, "To gain it is as if it had always been here;

to lose it is as if it had never been there. I only pray that the Venerable One will hold the burner and burn incense to make offerings to the Buddhas, so that in birth after birth we may advance toward Bodhi and always be good friends. The śramaṇa felt ashamed and returned the incense burner. Previously, there was a śramaṇa...
The four monks, including Men Sengshuo, had traveled from Xian’an to visit the Twin Sala Trees. Out of arrogance, they did not pay their respects.
Suddenly, they saw the Great Being’s body standing over ten feet tall, its golden hue radiating brilliantly; they could not help but prostrate themselves, vowing to become his disciples.
Later, they followed him into the capital, where he resided at Dinglin Temple on Mount Jiangshan. One day, they saw a white light before the Great Being’s seat and wondered what it was.
He saw a white felt cloth. He reached out his hand to take it, but the light returned to the Great Being (Mahāsattva), and there was nothing left to be found.
The Great Being said, "Henceforth, even if you see anything, do not attempt to take it. At that time, at Dinglin Monastery, the grasses and trees constantly rained down nectar.

Various insects came to feed upon it, and people gathered like clouds; many were killed and injured. The Great Being wished to move to another location, but that night, the dew ceased and the insects vanished.
He departed, and [the assembly] subsequently ceased. Soon after, he returned to Yunhuang.
In the first year of the Tianjia era, his disciples Huirong and others wished to establish a Longhua Assembly (Dragon Flower Assembly).

The Great Being said, "You may instead organize an 'Assembly for Requesting the Buddha to Halt His Radiance. The Dragon Flower Assembly is my own affair. If you follow my words, you will certainly behold the Dragon Flower."
The Great Being spoke again: "I attained the Way forty kalpas ago, whereas Śākyamuni Buddha only recently resolved his mind [upon enlightenment].
It is because he was able to renounce his body and practice asceticism that he attained Buddhahood before me."
In the second year of the Tianjia era, the Great Being was practicing the Way on the mountain. He constantly saw the seven Buddhas before him and Vimalakīrti following behind.
Thereupon, he said to his disciples: "Among the seven Buddhas, only Śākyamuni frequently converses with me; the other Buddhas do not."
It was thus repeatedly. He asked: "Why do the other Buddhas not speak? He replied: "Śākyamuni is currently presiding over this world, and I am to succeed him;
for this reason, the World-Honored One speaks with me frequently. He asked: "Why do you not see the Buddhas of other directions, but see only these seven Buddhas?
He replied: "Although the seven Buddhas have passed away long ago, because they collectively presided over this [world],"
This is because of the nature of the world. Question: Does the Great Being know what is being thought within the minds of others? Answer: No.

I constantly roam within the ultimate principle of non-arising (anutpāda), which is far superior to that of the past. Question: The Sūtra says: "Once received, one does not regress; one is eternally tranquil."
"What is meant by the loss of the knowledge of past lives? He replied, "I am now an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and thus there is arising and ceasing.

Nevertheless, within this process, the beginning and end are not lost. At present they are not fully possessed; it is only when I appear at the Tree of Enlightenment that they shall be fully possessed."

However, when his disciples travel afar and are about to return, they themselves know the day of their arrival; this is merely a minor supernormal power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*).
There was a Dharma Master named Hui who wished to test the Great Being (Mahāsattva). He led more than eighty people and suddenly arrived to beg for food.

The Great Being’s regular meal provided only enough for four people. Miaoguang was worried about this, but as the Great Being personally distributed the rice with his own hands, the entire multitude was fully satiated.
It is complete.

On the twelfth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Tianjia era, the Great Being again offered five hundred *hu* of rice and thirty bundles of silk to sponsor a Dharma assembly, and then spoke this verse:
I have heard in secret that the Buddha-dharma is about to perish; My grief and fear are indeed difficult to bear.

Only when the burdens of such clinging are exhausted does one finally awaken to the Way and realize the Unsurpassed Truth, which is truly non-dual.

For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, out of great compassion and pity, open the gates of skillful means and constantly exhort others to leave the household life. There are two aspects to the dharma of leaving home: first, the renunciation of form.
There are two types of renunciation: renunciation of the body and renunciation of the mind. Renunciation of the body refers to shaving off the hair and beard so as to accord with the Dharma-body.
Renunciation of the mind refers to departing from all objects of attachment and the bonds of existence. If we consider this in terms of the present life alone, renunciation of the body is superior.
Why? Because one is not led away by private or public affairs; being uniquely liberated and free from entanglements, one dwells in serene independence. If...

From the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva*), there are no two [distinctions]. Furthermore, there is renunciation through phenomena (*dharma*) and renunciation through principle. Regarding renunciation through phenomena:

it is renouncing the household of stinginess, the household of greed, the household of anger, the household of killing, the household of devouring sentient beings, the household of theft, the household of sexual misconduct, the household of harming others for one’s own benefit, the household of frivolous speech and falsehood, and the household of harsh speech.

Families of double-tongued speech; families that give rise to envy of the virtuous and jealousy of the capable; families that give rise to hatred and attachment; families that give rise to enmity and intimacy; families that give rise to mutual contention over superiority and inferiority;

families that give rise to mutual disparagement and replacement; families that give rise to mutual fighting and beating; families that give rise to arrogance and conceit; families that give rise to "I" and "mine";

families that give rise to a lack of benevolence and filial piety; families that give rise to shamelessness and lack of remorse; families that give rise to violating kindness and turning one's back on righteousness; families that give rise to non-... [incompleteness in source].

It issues from the family of humility; it issues from the family of freedom from slander; it issues from the family of freedom from disparagement; it issues from the family of that which is contrary to worldly reason;
it issues from the family of non-reverence; it issues from the family of the six sense objects; it issues from the family of all forms of pride; it issues from the family of the pride of "I am";

it issues from the family of false pride; it issues from the family of arrogance; it issues from the family of haughtiness; it issues from the family of the pride of inferiority; it issues from the family of the pride of equality; it issues from the family of increasing...

They emerge from the arrogance of high birth; they emerge from the arrogance of being learned and widely knowledgeable; they emerge from the arrogance of observing the precepts; they emerge from the arrogance of meditative concentration;

they emerge from the arrogance of [venerating] teachers; they emerge from the arrogance of [venerating] the Saṃgha; they emerge from the arrogance of nobility; they emerge from the arrogance of wealth; they emerge from the arrogance of physical beauty;
they emerge from the arrogance of being a man; they emerge from the arrogance of power; they emerge from the arrogance of artistic skill; they emerge from the arrogance of the burning house.
To depart from the home of the three realms and to depart from the home of all conditioned fetters—this is called the "departure by deed.
What faults exist within this home, this dwelling, such that one must renounce it?

Indeed, within this home, this dwelling, there are immeasurable enemies and creditors who hold swords and blades in their hands, constantly waiting for me to come so as to kill and harm my body; therefore, one must renounce it. Furthermore:
There are immeasurable tigers, wolves, and lions that constantly await my arrival to devour my body; I must therefore seek liberation from them.
Furthermore, there are many evil snakes, centipedes, and their like that constantly await my arrival to afflict and harm my body; I must therefore seek liberation from them.
Moreover, there are the various sufferings of the three miserable realms and the hells, which constantly await my arrival to inflict tortures upon me.
I must bring this body to liberation. Furthermore, there are many masters who constantly await my arrival to employ my body for their service.
What are these masters? The mind of stinginess is a master; the mind of greed is a master; the mind of anger is a master;
the mind of harmful intent is a master; the mind that devours sentient beings is a master; the mind of theft is a master; and the mind of perversion...

The mind of lust is the master. The mind that harms others to benefit oneself is the master. The mind of flowery speech and false words is the master. The mind of harsh speech and double-tongued slander is the master.
The mind of jealousy toward the virtuous and envy of the capable is the master. The mind of hatred and attachment is the master.
The mind of enmity and kinship is the master. The mind of "self" and "other" is the master. The mind of mutual contention for victory and defeat is the master.
The mind that seeks to overpower others is the master. The mind that seeks to contend and strike out at others is the master.
The mind of arrogance is the master. The mind of self-centeredness is the master. The mind lacking compassion and filial piety is the master. The mind devoid of shame and remorse is the master.
The mind that violates kindness and betrays righteousness is the master. The mind lacking humility and deference is the master.
The mind of slander is the master. The mind of mutual disparagement is the master. The mind of unrighteousness in the world is the master.
The mind of lack of reverence is the master. The mind of the six sense objects is the master. All minds of pride are the master.
The eye’s craving for gorgeous colors is the master. The ear’s craving for improper sounds is the master.
The master: The nose’s craving for unrighteous fragrances is the master; the tongue’s craving for unrighteous flavors is the master;
the body’s craving for smooth textures is the master; the mind’s taking of evil objects as its condition is the master;
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely masters. These various masters can employ one, can revile one, can strike one, and can bind one fast.
They can bind me with shackles and chains; they can kill me; they can boil and roast me; they can devour my body.
In this world, there are those who serve others as their subordinates, yet even they still say it is "hardship" and that it is "unbearable.

How much more so for one bound to such a master, enduring all manner of suffering—is it truly bearable? Therefore, one must seek liberation. One who leaves the home life according to principle... leaves.
The Noble Eightfold Path issues from the house of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; it issues from the house of the eighteen unique qualities;

it issues from the house of the five eyes; it issues from the house of the six supernormal powers; it issues from the house of the three knowledges; it issues from the house of the knowledge of others' minds; it issues from the house of the knowledge of past lives;

it issues from the house of great compassion and great loving-kindness; it issues from the house of equanimity; it issues from the house of the perfectly realized wisdom of awakening; it issues from the Buddha.
The Dharma and the Sangha—this is called "leaving home through principle.
Someone may ask: "If there is such a thing as leaving home, is there also 'entering home'? Now, I shall briefly explain entering home:

entering the home of universal quiescence, entering the home of great movement, entering the home of manifesting physical forms, and entering the home of non-abiding. If one acts in this way, that is indeed the Great [Vehicle]."
Vehicle. Why is this? If one uses non-arising to obstruct arising, that person is far removed from non-arising;

if one uses non-extinction to obstruct extinction, that person is far removed from non-extinction. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Birth-and-death is nirvāṇa," because there is no falling back and no arising.
Why is there no falling back and no arising? Because there is nowhere from which it comes. Why is there nowhere from which it comes? Because...
Because there is nowhere to which one goes. Why is it that there is nowhere to which one goes? Because it is to remain far removed from existence within the three periods of time.

Why is it that one remains far removed from existence within the three periods of time? Because it is to accord with the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Why is it that one accords with the nature of all phenomena?

Because it is for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, leading them equally to nirvana. Therefore, although one attains the Buddha-way and turns the wheel of Dharma, [one does not...]
One abandons the path to enlightenment. Why? Because one does not make the original vow in vain.
It is asked: What is meant by "coming from nowhere"? It means not relying on any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What is meant by "going nowhere"? It means not grasping at any dharmas. What is meant by "being far removed from past existence"? It means not...
Abiding in the tracks of the past, one is free from names and designations because there is nothing to be clearly distinguished. What is meant by being far removed from existence in the present?
It means that the present mind is not defiled by the two dharmas of existence and non-existence. What is meant by being far removed from existence in the future?

It means that the mind does not grasp at the future, having realized the unconditioned nature of phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). What is meant by being far removed from existence in the three periods of time? It is for the sake of exhausting all existence.
It is for the sake of all phenomena, because they are unattainable; it is for the sake of conforming to the nature of all phenomena, because it is to abide in non-abiding.

What is meant by abiding in non-abiding? It is for the sake of giving rise to infinite great kindness and great compassion. What is meant by giving rise to infinite great kindness and great compassion?
It is for the sake of teaching and transforming all sentient beings so that they equally attain nirvana. What is meant by accomplishing *anuttara*... [bodhi]?
Samyaksaṃbodhi refers to the realization of the quiescent unconditioned by being detached from all conditioned phenomena.
Why is it that one does not "attain" anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? It is because one does not abide in any forms of quiescence for the sake of all phenomena.
What is meant by "attaining the non-attainable"? It is because one does not attain the duality of existence and non-existence, abiding like space in a state of non-abiding.
Question: As stated above, one who has severed all攀緣 (pān-yuan, objects of attachment), is ultimately undefiled, and is not led astray by the fetters (saṃyojana) is already liberated.
Why, then, is it necessary to practice seated meditation, fix the mind, and count the breaths? Answer: Seated meditation and counting the breaths are the initial gateway for entering the Path.
This is precisely because the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of sentient beings are stubborn and they deeply crave the five desires (pañca-kāmaguṇa). Due to these afflictions...

The afflictions are blazing and intense; they cause frustration and lack of composure. Therefore, through the skillful means of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one is instructed to bind the mind to the counting of breaths, thereby suspending mental anxieties and preventing the mind from focusing on coarse and evil worldly matters.

Furthermore, one is led to contemplate the faults and sufferings of the body, developing weary detachment from birth and death, and to practice with diligent effort for many days and years. Once this practice has continued for a long time, the objects of attachment gradually subside, and the mind attains [tranquility].
Being pliant and supple, one is then able to sever all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), such as stinginess, greed, and hatred.
Once these formations are exhausted, the mind accords with the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and realizes tranquil unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*); this is called attaining the Way (*mārga*).

Even if a person practices seated meditation and focuses the mind on counting the breaths, if they do not sever conditioned formations such as hatred, they will ultimately not attain the Way. Why is this so? Because the Way is...

Regarding unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*): all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are causes for the conditioned. Now, to practice the causes of the conditioned while hoping for the fruit of the unconditioned—is this not difficult?
Furthermore, regarding the three vehicles and the demonic activities of non-Buddhists, it is said: first, as for the Śrāvaka vehicle, they are unable to provide universal salvation.

One merely contemplates the afflictions of the body, develops weary detachment from birth and death, severs all conditioned fetters and attachments, settles the mind in the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and realizes the quiescence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is called the Śrāvaka vehicle. Second, as for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle: one develops weary detachment from birth and death.
Severing all attachments to conditioned phenomena and their fetters, one practices the four immeasurables and the six perfections to extensively save all sentient beings.
Settling the mind in the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) to attain realization, one manifests the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics of a Buddha; this is the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
Third, as for the Mahāyāna: it quiets all攀緣 (pān-yuan) [conceptual clinging] and the various fetters of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
One practices the four immeasurables and the six perfections to extensively save all sentient beings, treating enemies and kin with equality, and dedicating [merit] toward *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Yet, one does not realize *samyak-saṃbodhi* while practicing all dharmas, remaining detached from the marks of all dharmas. Therefore, it is neither mundane nor non-mundane; it is neither nirvāṇa—
It is not that there is no nirvāṇa; it is neither bound nor liberated. It serves eternally as the parent of the triple world, extensively saving all sentient beings until the end of the future.

This is called the Mahāyāna. What is meant by the karma of external paths? The karma of external paths consists of cultivating tainted (sāsrava) goodness, loathing the lower realms while grasping for the higher, practicing various ascetic penances, and also cultivating various merits, in the hope of attaining high elevation and sovereignty, and receiving [rewards] forever.
"Unconditioned peace and happiness—this is the work of non-Buddhists.
Question: "All things that arise must die; all undertakings that succeed must fail. If one generates the mind to pursue the Way, how can one attain long-lasting, eternal bliss?
What constitutes the work of Māra? Answer: "It is conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). What are these formations? The mind of stinginess is a formation."
Grounds. A mind of greed is a ground of activity. A mind of killing is a ground of activity. A mind of devouring sentient beings is a ground of activity.

A mind of theft is a ground of activity. A mind of anger is a ground of activity. A mind of malicious envy is a ground of activity. A mind that harms others for one’s own benefit is a ground of activity.
A mind of frivolous play is a ground of activity. A mind of song and dance is a ground of activity. Frivolous speech and falsehood...

The mind that harbors malice is a ground for action. The mind that engages in harsh speech and double-tongued talk is a ground for action. The mind that is envious and jealous of the virtuous is a ground for action.
The mind of love and hatred is a ground for action. The mind of "self" and "other" is a ground for action. The mind that contends with one another over victory and defeat is a ground for action.
The mind that seeks to oppress and destroy one another is a ground for action. The mind that fights and strikes one another is a ground for action. All forms of prideful mind are grounds for action.

This is the ground of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra-bhūmi*). A mind of "I" and "mine" is the ground of conditioned activity. A mind lacking loving-kindness and filial piety is the ground of conditioned activity.

A mind devoid of shame and dread of blame is the ground of conditioned activity. A mind that violates kindness and turns its back on righteousness is the ground of conditioned activity. A mind lacking humility and deference is the ground of conditioned activity.

A mind of mutual slander is a ground for practice. A mind of disparagement is a ground for practice. A worldly mind that is contrary to reason is a ground for practice. A mind lacking reverence is a ground for practice.
An eye that craves beautiful and brilliant forms is a ground for practice. An ear that craves unrighteous sounds is a ground for practice.
A nose that craves unrighteous fragrances is a ground for practice. A tongue that craves what is unreasonable... [is a ground for practice].
The taste of these things is the realm of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra-bhūmi*). The body’s craving for smoothness and softness is the realm of conditioned activity.
The mind’s taking of evil objects as its conditions is the realm of conditioned activity. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whether wholesome or unwholesome, are the works of Māra.

These conditioned activities circulate through birth and death without rest; they constantly dwell in a dark house through the long night of eternal kalpas, devoid of light. One must urgently distance oneself from them.
[He] departs. Again, he asks: "What is meant by 'Māra'? He replies: "Māra means 'perversity. To give rise to a mind that grasps at the external is perversity;
to give rise to a mind that grasps at the internal is perversity; to give rise to a mind that grasps at that which is between is perversity. If the mind does not..."
When one is born, there is no movement. If the mind does not move, that is correctness. Again, he asked:
"For what reason do people transmigrate through birth and death without rest? He replied: "Transmigration through birth and death is not caused by another;
it is entirely brought about by the karma of one's own body, speech, and mind. Therefore, one must..."
One must control the sense faculties and not allow them to become heedless. Some people say: "Once dead, what more can one know?
Death and life are no different from one another. Why is this so? For all who possess a body, it is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) unites with the physical form and pervades its entirety. That which currently allows one to perceive cold and heat, and to experience suffering and pleasure, is entirely due to this.
That which is known is known by the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna-ātman*); it is not known by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

If you say this is not so, why is it that after the consciousness-spirit has departed, the corpse does not know pleasure or pain? By inferring from this, it is clear that death and life are no different;
it is simply the consciousness-spirit that experiences suffering and pleasure. If today one cannot endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, burning and boiling, or being cut and sliced...
If one roasts [a living being], they will suffer pain; later, they will enter hell—how could they possibly endure it?
If one refuses to discipline the mind to do good, but instead indulges in killing sentient beings and committing various evils, then upon death one will enter the three miserable realms and hells:

the mountain of knives and trees of swords, the boiling cauldrons and glowing embers, the copper pillars and iron beds, the sawing and grinding, the river of ashes and the boiling excrement, and the Avīci Hell of Cold.
How could one endure such various and manifold sufferings? A verse on the Five Sufferings from the Daoist tradition says:
Falling into the realm of spirits is the suffering of birth; One revolves through the courtyard of the five paths. Long confined in the eternal night, for kalpas there has been no light;
Upon the mountain of blades and the many sword-trees, Poisonous weapons jostle one another in their jagged heights.
Above, there are those who tread upon the hoarfrost, Whose moments know no temporary rest. Hungry, they eat iron pellets and charcoal;
thirsty, they drink the essence of smelting fires. Wandering through the three miserable realms, how could they recognize form or name?
Thinking of you who do not understand destiny—how bitter it is! It wounds my heart.
Furthermore, some say: "The people of the world who study the Way do not all subsist on a vegetarian diet; why does the Mahāsattva alone adhere to a vegetarian diet?
He replied: "What is meant by the 'Noble Way' (āryamārga)? The Noble Way is correctness (samyaktva). First is correctness of principle (li-zheng), and second is correctness of the world (shi-zheng).
A person who studies the Way should cultivate correctness of principle. As for correctness of principle, the mind is neither within nor..."
It is not outside, nor is it in between; the mind is purely tranquil, like empty space.

If one gives rise to thoughts of craving for the worldly flavors that are contrary to principle, how can that be considered correct? Second, a person who studies the Way should cultivate worldly correctness.
Worldly correctness means: when noble, do not oppress the lowly; when wealthy, do not oppress the poor; when wise, do not oppress the ignorant; when strong, do not...
To oppress the weak. For this reason, one should not speak what is not correct, nor act in ways that are not the Way.
If one desires to diminish the benefit of others to enrich oneself, how can this be considered correct? Furthermore, all classes of animals are created by those who have committed transgressions;
