they themselves consider themselves to lack power and influence, unable to protect or defend one another. Now, for the sake of craving their flesh, do you instead assist in their torment and oppression? First, it violates compassion; second—
This is contrary to reason. Thirdly, this is also the root of sinful karma and the cycle of birth and death.

For what reason do all people transmigrate through manifold sufferings without rest? It is because they do not employ the principles of the Way themselves, but instead treat one another with contempt and usurpation, and kill and harm each other.
Because of this, they wander through the three miserable realms and the hells, undergoing immeasurable suffering. Therefore, one should resolve the mind to maintain a vegetarian diet until the end.

"Life does not transfer. Furthermore, someone asked: "If one consumes a vegetarian diet for a long time, it may cause illness; what is the nature of this matter? He replied: "For what reason do people fall ill?
It is simply because they committed various evils in their past lives, which have brought about the suffering of illness in the present. If one now..."
One commits various evils and, furthermore, incurs the suffering of illness in the future. It is like a person who, because of an old wound, stabs his body with a fresh, sharp thorn;
due to the pain of that [old] wound, he then stabs himself with a new, sharp one. How could this ever lead to recovery?

One must extract the old thorn and refrain from stabbing with a new one; only then will the pain be healed. What is meant by "extracting the old thorn and refraining from stabbing with a new one"? It means:
For sins already committed, I take refuge in the Triple Gem and openly confess them; for evils not yet committed, I vow never to commit them again.
By doing so, one shall obtain freedom from further suffering and affliction throughout all future lives.
He asked again: "What is the nature of seeking wealth through unrighteous means to make offerings to the Triple Gem? He replied:
"I have heard it said in the sutras that if one makes a Buddha out of wealth acquired through unrighteous means, it is not permitted to pay homage to such a Buddha.
By this inference, we know that the Buddha did not permit people to harm sentient beings in order to seek profit and make offerings to the Triple Gem."
Furthermore, some say: "Our entire family abstains from killing; we simply always eat meat that has already died. How should this matter be regarded? The answer is:
If the eater does not cease, the killer will not stop either. If the eater ceases, the killing will naturally stop as well.
Someone asked: "I have committed many evil deeds, yet I am able to extensively read and recite the various sutras.
The sutras state that one who can read and recite even a single phrase or a single verse can extinguish boundless heavy sins and increase boundless merit.
How should this statement be understood? He replied: "This is the compassionate skillful means of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; therefore, they use it to entice and encourage those before them."

The severance [of evil] comes later. If sentient beings read the scriptures and their minds attain realization of the Way, distancing themselves from all evils and transforming their hearts toward goodness, then even a single phrase or a single verse can truly extinguish boundless heavy sins and increase boundless merit.

If one now recites many scriptures extensively but the mind does not cease its evils, one will likewise be unable to extinguish sin or generate blessings. How may this be verified? I venture to say...
I have heard that the two bhikṣus Shanxing (Sunakṣatra) could recite and chant the twelve divisions of the honored sūtras as fluently as pouring water;

yet, because they harbored evil and did not abide in it, they were reborn in their very bodies within the Avīci Great Hell. Inferring from this, one knows that although there is much learning and recitation, [if it is not accompanied by practice, it is of no avail].
If the mind does not cease from evil, one will ultimately be unable to extinguish transgressions and generate merit.

Someone asked: "In this world, there are people who constantly lecture on the sutras and the vinaya; they know what is evil yet do not treat it as evil, and they know what is a transgression yet do not treat it as such."

One knows what constitutes an offense and what does not. Furthermore, while one can externally maintain a disciplined and orderly demeanor, if internally one does not cease various unwholesome actions, how can this principle be reconciled?

Can such a person attain liberation from all suffering? The answer is: Suppose there is a person who internally fully understands the causes and effects, as well as the conditions for suffering and pleasure, and whose external form is likewise able to maintain a disciplined and orderly demeanor; yet, they are unable to love themselves. Still...
If five hundred iron mallets were placed inside one's clothing, what do you think? Would this person be able to remain free from pain?

It is the same with those who study the Way today: though they may outwardly maintain a disciplined and dignified demeanor, if they do not sever their various evil deeds within their hearts, the consequence will be that they later fall into the hands of their enemies and are bound in dark prisons to undergo manifold sufferings.

Suffering is without limit. How could one possibly be beset by such agony? I pray that all you virtuous ones will further exhort one another to concentrate the mind on a single point, sever the攀緣 (pān-yuan—clinging to objects) of all conditioned formations, reach ultimate non-defilement, and cause the mind to become empty and tranquil.

When one darkly accords with the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one immediately attains liberation from all suffering and transcends to realize the unconditioned, eternal bliss. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The path that extinguishes suffering is truly the authentic path; there is no other path."
It is further said: Suppose there is a person who suffers from the illness of the six desires and seeks a teacher to receive the precepts.

Once the precepts have been received, if they do not uphold them, will the illness be cured? The answer is: It is like a person suffering from a severe illness who seeks out a skilled physician and searches for excellent medicine;
yet, though the patient repeatedly reads the prescription, they do not take the medicine. This is the case among all people.
"How is it? Will this illness ever be cured? It is just the same with people today who receive the precepts but do not uphold them.
If they do not eliminate the causes of the six desires, they will inevitably bear the fruit of the sixty types of *caṇḍāla* conduct in the future.
Dragged by these sixty types of conduct, they transmigrate through birth and death, taking countless lives.
Question: From what do these outcaste-like conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-cāṇḍāla*) arise? Answer: If one craves forms, they are precisely feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
If one craves sounds, they are precisely feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. If one craves odors, they are precisely feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.
If one craves tastes, they are precisely feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. If one craves tangibles, they are precisely feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

If the mind craves worldly phenomena, these are precisely feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Thus, with five [elements] present within one, and five times six making thirty, there are thirty *caṇḍālas*.

If one craves supramundane form, it is precisely feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. If one craves supramundane sound, it is precisely feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
If one craves supramundane fragrance, it is precisely feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. If one craves supramundane...

The flavors of the world are precisely feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. If one craves supramundane contact, it is precisely feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
If one craves supramundane dharmas, it is precisely feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Thus, within each of these there are five; five times six makes thirty.
Together with the previous [sixty], they total sixty *caṇḍālas*. What is meant by "supramundane flavor and contact"? It refers to craving for *nirvāṇa* and attachment.
This is the arising of the Dharma. These sixty types of *cāṇḍāla* formations should be avoided.
The wise person must observe them with careful and thorough reflection, so that the mind is neither external, nor internal, nor in between—just like empty space, having no point of reliance.
Thus one attains liberation from the suffering of birth and death and realizes the eternal bliss of true *nirvāṇa*.

Someone may raise this objection: "It is commonly taught that performing good deeds brings about happiness; why then are there people in the world who practice virtue yet instead encounter poverty and suffering?

The answer is: "Most of these are great *mahā-upāya* bodhisattvas who, out of compassion and for the sake of universal salvation, manifest themselves to practice virtue while undergoing manifold sufferings.

The more they are distressed, the firmer they become; they do not crave worldly pleasures, but diligently repent, wishing only to relinquish their bodies so as to bring about a vision [of the truth]."

The Buddhas act thus for what reason? It is precisely because sentient beings have newly resolved their minds on the Way (*bodhicitta*), yet their faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is not yet established;
they frequently encounter obstacles and adversaries, and there is fear that their resolve for the Way might regress or perish.

To lead them toward firmness and cause them to advance toward the Buddha-way, the sutra speaks of repenting former sins rather than speaking of past liberation. By means of his own illness, he takes pity upon the illnesses of others.
Furthermore, an objection is raised: "It is commonly taught that committing evil brings about suffering.

Why is it that some people in this world are born with a disposition for evil, yet in their present life they enjoy wealth, honor, and peace, with their descendants filling their halls? The answer is: "When a person attains wealth and honor, it does not result from a single lifetime.
It arises from having practiced generosity and extensively cultivated merit in previous lives; the fruit of that retribution is experienced as wealth and honor in this present life."
Peace and happiness. Although one may commit evil in this life, one does not immediately experience the suffering. It is like a person who kills a hundred people;
those hundred harbor a heavy resentment and constantly desire to take revenge. However, because they are guarded by a thousand men, they find no opportunity.
They intend to wait until the thousand have departed, so that they may seize and kill the hundred, thereby undergoing immeasurable suffering.
He asked again: "Regarding the animal realm, how does their affection for and attachment to their kin compare to that of humans? He replied:
"Although their forms differ and their bodies are distinct, when it comes to craving life and fearing death, their feelings of intimacy and affection are no different from those of humans.
Now, humans claim to possess the eye of wisdom and perceive the paths of suffering and joy within birth and death, yet they still commit the five pains and the five burnings."
Because they have endured various sufferings and afflictions throughout the long night of eternal kalpas without respite, yet do not know how to distance themselves from them—
can they still be called wise?
The Great Being spoke again to the people, saying: "For what reason do you all constantly suffer the pains and burnings of the five afflictions?
It is surely because you yourselves have created the causes for these five pains and five burnings. It is like a person who has five hundred iron spikes driven into their body."

The entire body suffers from pain day and night, unbearable to endure. Now, for the sake of you virtuous ones, I wish to extract this affliction so that your bodies and minds may be at peace and free from further suffering.
What do you think? Would you prefer it extracted by means of a staircase, or would you prefer it extracted all at once?
What is meant by extraction by means of a staircase? It is when someone receives and upholds the Three Refuges in the Buddha and the precept against killing, observing them for a month.

The six fast days (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa*). Eating vegetarian food on the fast days is like pulling out one hundred roots. There is a person who upholds the Buddha’s five precepts, observes the six fast days each month, and eats vegetarian food on those fast days;

this is like pulling out two hundred roots. There is a person who upholds the Buddha’s ten wholesome precepts, observes the six fast days each month, observes the three long fasts (*trīṇi dīrghopavāsāni*) each year, and eats vegetarian food on those fast days; this is like pulling out three hundred roots. There is a person who upholds the Buddha’s...

The precepts of the śrāvakas consist of: refraining from all evil, practicing all that is good, abstaining from meat at all times, and practicing the Way during the six periods of the day—this is likened to pulling out four hundred strong men.
Furthermore, there is one who upholds the Buddha’s and Bodhisattvas’ precepts, refraining from all evil.

Practice all that is good. Observe lifelong vegetarianism during the long months. Practice the Way throughout the six periods of the day. Cherish and protect the True Dharma, not sparing even one's own body or life.

Exalt and propagate the Holy Path, widely transforming all sentient beings so that they may together attain liberation. This is likened to pulling out five hundred strong men at once; it is what is meant by "pulling them out together.
Now, you virtuous ones, for what reason do you indulge your hearts in creating evil? Upon death, you will enter the three miserable realms and the hells, where you shall suffer without end.
If one can discipline the mind toward goodness, after the end of this life, one will be reborn above in the heavens within a palace of the seven treasures.

One’s appearance will be upright and handsome, with extraordinary and sublime marks; one will be honored, noble, wealthy, and powerful, possessing sovereign mastery. Whatever one desires to obtain, it shall be fulfilled according to one's thoughts.
There are silver ponds at the four gates, and groves and gardens where jeweled trees resound; flowers and leaves provide lush shade and reflection.
Fragrant breezes waft and flutter; golden branches and jade leaves play various wondrous melodies that delight the human heart, providing joy for eternal kalpas.
The verse says:
The mind is tamed as an ox-cart, Leading people to the Brahma Heaven. Within the various palaces of the Brahma Heaven,
All are self-luminous, like flowers in the spring month; Their manifold colors delight the human heart.
Those who love these flowers Shall forever be free from the entanglements of all dust.
*Śubhavyūha Bodhisattva Record*, Volume Two.
Record of the Great Being Shanhui, Volume Three:
Four Verses on the Arising of Phenomena (Samskāra)
Consciousness relies upon the floating bubble to arise; birth comes from craving and desire. Having once been full-grown in former times, one is now again an infant.

Star-like eyes follow others as they turn; crimson lips open toward the breast. Because of being deluded regarding the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one returns once more to undergo the cycle of saṃsāra.

Old age: Beholding one’s reflection in the mirror, the countenance has changed; ascending the steps, one’s strength has declined. Alas! Now that I am old, my ability to perform prostrations and obeisances has diminished.
My body is like a tree on a precipice; my mind is like a tortoise dwelling in water. Yet I still remain addicted to outflows (*āsrava*), unwilling to study the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
Suddenly beset by the signs of illness, one falls into a deep and lingering malady, thereby becoming a bedridden patient. Wife and children grieve in silence; friends weary of such intimacy.
As agonizing pain pulls at every fiber of the body, the moaning reaches all four neighbors. Yet, unaware of the perils ahead, one still indulges freely in greed and anger.

The vital spirit of the dying departs the path of life; the wandering soul enters the barrier of death. One hears only of thousands and tens of thousands departing, yet never sees a single person return.
The fine steed stands neighing in vain; the courtyard flowers can never again be plucked. Seek the Unsurpassed Way early, and you shall surely escape the mountains of the four quarters.
Inscription on the Mind-King:
Contemplating the King of the Empty Mind— Mysterious and wondrous, difficult to fathom; Formless and signless, yet possessing great supernatural power.
It can extinguish a thousand calamities and accomplish ten thousand virtues. Though its essential nature is empty, it is able to bestow the Dharma rules.
Behold it—formless; call upon it—it has sound. It acts as the General of the Great Dharma; the Mind-precept transmits the Sūtras.
Like the flavor of salt in water, like the clarity of glue within color: It definitely exists, yet its form is not seen. The King of the Mind is likewise:
Dwelling within the body, Entering and exiting through the gate of the face, Responding to things according to circumstances.
Sovereign and unimpeded, all that is done is accomplished. Realizing the fundamental consciousness-mind, one sees the Buddha through the consciousness-mind.
This mind is the Buddha; this Buddha is the mind. In every thought, it is the Buddha-mind; the Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha.
If you wish to achieve success early, discipline yourself with the precept-mind. Purify the precepts and purify the mind; the mind itself is the Buddha.
Apart from this mind-king, there is no other Buddha. If you wish to attain Buddhahood, do not defile yourself with a single thing.
Although the nature of the mind is empty, the essence of greed and hatred is real. Enter this Dharma-gate and, sitting upright, attain Buddhahood.
Having reached the other shore, you will obtain the *pāramitās*. Those who aspire to the Way should observe their own minds.
Know that the Buddha is within; do not seek him outwardly. This very mind is the Buddha, and this very Buddha is the mind.
When the mind clearly recognizes the Buddha, and one understands and recognizes the mind, one realizes that apart from the mind there is no Buddha, and apart from the Buddha there is no mind.
If one cannot fathom this non-duality of Buddha and mind, one will be incapable of anything. Clinging to emptiness and stagnating in quiescence, one will drift and sink therein.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not find peace of mind through this; it is the Great Being who clarifies the mind who awakens to this profound resonance.
The nature of body and mind is wondrous, and its functioning undergoes no alteration. Therefore, the wise let the mind rest in freedom.
Do not speak of a "mind-king" that is empty and devoid of substantiality, yet which can cause the physical body to act either erroneously or correctly.
Neither existent nor non-existent, its appearance and concealment are indeterminate; though the nature of mind is empty, it can manifest as both ordinary and sagely.
Therefore, I exhort you: take care to guard yourself with vigilance. Every moment of action leads once more to drifting and sinking.
The pure mind-intelligence is like the gold of the world; the treasury of Prajñā resides within both body and mind.
The unconditioned jewel of the Dharma is neither shallow nor deep; all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas realize this original mind.
For those who encounter it through a karmic affinity, it is neither of the past, future, nor present.
Furthermore, a verse says:
Surveying the four great oceans and gazing upon the mountains of the five aggregates, the place where the Tathāgata practiced the Way is profoundly serene in its numinous wisdom.
The jeweled palace shines with bright pearls, and the flowered seat is fresh with beautiful jade. The Mind-King clarifies the teachings of the Dharma, spreading wide the lotus of Prajñā.
Pure ground, bodhi-seeds; may we attain the God among Gods. Contemplating within this physical body, the heart-king prajñā is empty.
It is the dwelling place of noble wisdom, yet the path of ordinary beings is not the same. Entering and exiting, there is no gate; searching for it, no trace is found.
The great body is vast and boundless; the subtle mind admits not a speck of dust. Desiring to reach the other shore, hoist high the sail of wisdom.
With the pure, luminous pearl of precepts, adorn the Buddha’s site of enlightenment. Let the body manifest the marks of the Tathāgata, and let the mind be the sovereign of Prajñā.
May you swiftly ascend the lotus throne; may your mouth emit a great, circular radiance that broadly illuminates boundless realms.

May you act as a bridge for all beings, opening the great Piṇi-piṭaka and spreading the fragrance of precepts and meditative concentration. May your insight penetrate the wisdom of non-arising; in the void, who comes and goes?
Forever transcending the prison of the three realms, unstained by the womb of the four māras, you sport upon the lotus and dwell securely on the terrace of the dharma-nature.
All devas and humans gaze up in reverence; in the silent void, they praise you as "Excellent. Those with the karmic affinity meet your vast transformation, and the wondrous gate of Prajñā opens.
Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning, one rises together with him. Walking or standing, he is ever present; sitting or reclining, we dwell together.
Not separated by even a hair’s breadth, they are like a body and its shadow. If you wish to know where the Buddha is, it is simply this very sound of your voice.
Quiescence is the root of the Dharma King; movement is the sprout of the Dharma King. Since nirvana is not far off, eternal abiding is likewise not remote.

To turn the mind is called the Pure Land; afflictions shall vanish at that very moment. Desiring to cross the ocean of the three miserable realms, diligently cultivate the bridge of the six perfections.

One will certainly attain perfect enlightenment, like waiting for the incoming tide. The hidden treasure does not depart from one's own body; the pearl is within the midst of one’s being. Simply realize it within the sphere of the mind;
do not seek it far away in external emptiness. All myriad phenomena share the same true nature; though there are a thousand manifestations, their essence is one and the same.
If a person understands this Dharma, what need is there to toil in search of it? The four modes of birth share one and the same essence; the six realms of existence ultimately converge in me.
Ignorance is itself the Buddha; afflictions need not be eliminated.

There is no need to crave greed, hatred, or delusion; just look at the fish playing in the azure depths of the pond. It is simply because they covet the bait on the hook that they swallow a single line into their mouths.

There is no need for anger; anger can summon the causes for rebirth in hell. Simply use the power of meditative concentration to subdue the winds and fires, and you will possess a majestic body of purple-golden hue.
There is no need for delusion; delusion is being deceived by the six thieves of ignorance. Evil karma is created by one's own body and mind; the ignorant and confused merely wear it as their garment.
Cast off the skin of an animal.
(10) I exhort you once more: concentrate your mind and constantly recollect the *pāramitās*; diligently cultivate the six perfections toward Bodhi. Amidst the five turbidities and the three...
The ointment emerges spontaneously.

I exhort you, secondly: when a person appears in this world, do not seek profit. Even if one should obtain it, it lasts but a brief moment; before long, in an instant, one returns to the Realm of the Dead (Hao-li).

Exhortation Three: A human body is difficult to obtain; one must feel great shame [for past negligence]. Constantly recite the Buddha’s name throughout the six periods of day and night; diligently cultivate the Three Jewels and proceed toward the monastery.
Exhortation Four: Strive with effort to perform virtuous deeds. Do not say that youth and vigor bring a fine appearance; you do not yet know what lies ahead.
Where is this place called "Cheng"?
I urge you five times to reflect: hell is truly suffering. Though one may display an air of dignity amidst wealth and honor before one's eyes, in a mere moment, one returns to the dust.
I exhort you on six points. First, do not eat the flesh of sentient beings. Unless it is the manifestation of a Bodhisattva, it is surely a kinsman from a previous life.
I exhort you on seven points. In all matters, nothing surpasses the necessity of truthfulness. To have three in the morning and four in the evening for no reason—how can this principle be maintained?
One's own person will ultimately meet with misfortune.
This is my eighth exhortation to you: those who eat meat are true rākṣasas. If you kill the bodies of others in this life, you shall be killed by their bodies in a future birth.
Exhortation to You, Nine: Heaven and hell exist with distinct clarity; do not encourage monks to consume wine and meat, lest you be without hands or feet for five hundred lifetimes.
Exhortation to You, Ten: I urge you to practice with urgency; in a single day your life may end and you enter the Yellow Springs, leaving behind father, mother, and wife.
My son, you have wept in vain.
Two verses:
Empty-handed, I grasp a hoe; On foot, I ride a water buffalo. The buffalo passes over the bridge; The bridge flows, but the water does not flow.
There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast. It is able to act as the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet does not wither away with the four seasons.
*Returning to the Source*, Twelve Chapters:
Returning to the source, birth-and-death and nirvana are equal. Because the mind is not impartial, the nature of dharmas appears to have highs and lows.
Return to the source; it is easy to speak of, but difficult to apply the mind. Prajñā has no form or appearance; how can one be taught to contemplate it?
Return to the source; if you wish to seek prajñā, it is easy: simply cease the mind of right and wrong, and great wisdom will naturally be perfected.
Return to the source; wherever you are, it may be a place of secluded dwelling. Nirvana and birth-and-death are one; afflictions are themselves Bodhi. Return to the source;
rely on what is seen and do not follow emotional attachments. The Dharma-nature has neither increase nor decrease; it is only through deluded speech that we speak of deficiency and fullness.
Return to the source; why seek it further? If you wish to attain true liberation, contemplate your own mind with rectitude.
Return to the source; the nature of the mind is inconceivable. Let not your aspiration be small, but make it great: a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru.
Return to the source; liberation is boundless. Blending one's light with all things, one is like space, unstained by the world.
Return to the source; why seek through gradual stages? The nature of phenomena has no before or after; cultivate it in a single thought-moment, at a single time.
Returning to the source, the nature of mind neither sinks nor floats; abiding securely in the King Samādhi, the myriad practices are all fully gathered.
Return to the source! Birth and death are originally a chaotic tangle; through arbitrary conceptualization, the void is taken for reality, and the six sense-faculties remain perpetually obscured.
Returning to the Source. The wine of Prajñā is clear and pure; it can cure the disease of afflictions. Drink of it yourself and exhort all sentient beings.
A Song of Floating Bubbles: "Have you not seen? Sudden rain flows across the courtyard when viewed from nearby. Upon the water, countless bubbles arise one after another. At the very first drop..."

Forming into a single drop, it breaks apart; how many times does it dissolve away, and how many times does it float up? These floating bubbles gather and disperse without end; though they differ in size, their forms and colors are alike.
Sometimes they suddenly arise and are called "floating bubbles," yet once dissolved, they return to being the original water.

The bubbles exist of themselves and vanish of themselves; whether resembling space or resembling form, they are all collectively termed "void. Ultimately, they are identical to illusory transformations and shadows.
Fools call it a "half-moon pearl. At this moment, I sigh for Layman Xian: upon seeing a bubble on the water, he realized the nature of birth and death;
the bustling human world is entirely but a name in vain. Borrowing the floating bubble as a metaphor, one perceives that in every thought-moment within the human realm there is much rise and fall.
Like a rushing stream flowing eastward, there is never a time when it ceases. I address those who are prosperous and powerful in this world: look at the passing of the years and months.
How long can one remain thus?
Alone, I have composed twenty verses on the solitary mountain.
My thatched hut and grass-roofed cottage are secure; bears and cubs play about me, and flying birds come together to feed.
Dwelling alone, for what purpose do you exert yourself so? With an uplifted mind, you seek your original nature; with resolute character, you master True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Sleeping alone, you delight in profound contemplation within stillness; resting from the objects of攀缘 (*pán-yuán*, conceptual clinging), you do not abide in the extremes of existence or non-existence.
Sitting alone, contemplate in stillness the non-self; straighten this body and mind. Through compassion, one becomes a *sattva*.
Dwelling in solitude, accord with your original vow as it should be. The Way is shown within the sutras; strike through and shatter the lord of ignorance.
Walking alone, one sees forms as if blind; the light body is transformed into its kind, crawling without ever being startled.
Playing alone, I ask: what is there within my mind? If you see indeterminate states dwelling in the mind, cut them off immediately to return to the meaning of Prajñā.
Going alone, wherever one encounters conditions, it is all deluded thought. Within the mind of deluded thought, there is frantic pursuit;
yet this very pursuit is not "going.
Returning alone, climbing mountains and crossing ridges—upon what does one rely? By the time one reaches that which is relied upon, it is found to have no fixed reality. Observe this closely.
What, then, is the purpose of objects?

They arise alone. I ask: what is it that my mind clings to? Upon examining the four phases of mental activity, none of them are found to arise. How could a thousand ends and ten thousand threads bind me?
Speaking to oneself: I ask what it is that my mind grasps. When clearly illuminated, even skillful explanations are all empty.
Who is the master of the throat, lips, and tongue?

This solitary sentiment is, in truth, detached from sound and name. Through the three contemplations within a single mind, one is detached from the myriad categories; even the thorny thickets and forests are [all empty].

Tranquil in himself, uniquely sublime, he has distanced himself from the capital and the marketplace. He pursues his original vow to realize non-arising; until non-arising is attained, he will never cease.
It is best to be alone. For the morning meal of Zen flavor, shrimp are not required. Accepting this humble food as it is offered, one takes the five aggregates as a temporary home.
To delight in solitude and seek the state of no-more-learning, one must urgently sever the cords of the three realms to escape the evils of hell.
It is best to be alone. Resolutely seek the Bodhisattva path; perform myriad practices for the sake of sentient beings, and do not yet grasp the treasure of Nirvana.
Observe alone: try taking worldly conditions and examine them; seize this realm of impermanence and direct the single principle toward the mind’s contemplation.
Solitary and wondrous—this is precisely learning non-action (*wuwei*). Reflecting back upon the many discursive thoughts, they are directed toward the pool of *nirvāṇa*.

Solitary and sufficient, my vow-mind is boundless. Within the Dharma-realm of enemies and kin, words are perfect and true; only then can the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) transform and nurture the multitudes.
He dwells alone, yet his mind stores up [wisdom] to act as a virtuous friend who ties the jewel within one's robe. Through kalpas, the roots of beings become increasingly mature.
At that time, the Great Being, together with his disciples, contemplates and observes day and night whether the practitioner has been born or not born.
Extinction yet not extinguished; ceasing the grasping after objects and entering the mark of dharmas—this is liberation.
He then composed five verses, saying:
I. A New Beginning Holding incense within the Buddha niche, I pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One. Mind upon mind has already reached the state beyond ending.
At the second watch, he sat cross-legged in quiet meditation and attained penetration into the absence of self and other; true suchness is neither one nor two.
During the third watch, he contemplated that phenomena are both empty and not empty, without arising or ceasing, their essence being identical to true suchness.
Before the fourth watch: Contemplating that phenomena have no conditions, the four propositions of true suchness are severed; how could the hundred negations trouble me further?
At the beginning of the fifth watch: I bow my head in worship to Suchness; I take refuge in that which has neither new nor old, which is neither unreal nor real.
The Twenty Poems on the Difficulties of the Traveler (with Preface) Now, the nature of the mind is empty and still;
its measure is equal to the Dharma-realm. Following suchness, it is beyond all marks; it is without action and without conditions.

It exists eternally in profound stillness, yet without abiding. The flow of phenomena fills the world, yet the ultimate principle does not shift. The wondrous Way returns to emptiness and is universally...

It is identical with all phenomena. The Dharma King governs this and speaks of its golden solidity. Thus it was said of old: "To manifest its characteristics, yet it cannot be fully expressed by words.
Nevertheless, it encompasses all things while not being subsumed by those things; its nature is not something separate from liberation.
Fundamentally there are no ten fetters; because they do not arise due to conditions, it is called "mysterious. Words cannot reach it, hence it is named "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*).

It is constantly in harmony with the world, yet it is not defiled by worldly dharmas. The mundane is its very substance, yet it is not dragged about by the mundane. Thus it is void, profound, and transcendentally wondrous;
empty, yet designated as vast and open. The mind has no fixed form yet manifests forms; although it possesses form, it remains unconditioned.

Yet it is without form; its dispersion and convergence have no fixed direction, being neither returning nor departing. Through gathering it does not contract, and through expanding it does not broaden.
This is not a material object, yet it possesses sound; it embodies the Great Sound while remaining rarely audible. Its nature is quiescent, empty, and profound.
Neither one nor two, it shines forth with vast clarity. It is luminous and radiant by itself, yet never for a moment does it exist as a discrete entity;

rather, its entire manifestation is present before us. Although it is thus manifest, it is difficult to practice and difficult to emulate. Subtler than a hair-tip, yet not minute; pervading the three thousand worlds, yet not long.
Its principle is without fixed determination; there is no hearing and no listening. Though non-existent, it is a shimmering radiance—birth and death.
It is serene and uncontrived; it does not arise from nourishment or cultivation. All classes of conscious beings share this same fundamental law.
To realize it is called *nirvāṇa*, yet those who do not know it describe it as a mere mental fabrication. This is the truth, beyond doubt. It can be supple and it can be firm;
in its vast perspective, the world cannot contain it. When thoughts cease, the entire body becomes one with it; it is the formless form, tranquil and still.

Profound and vast, when it comes to rest, it constitutes a body that is immeasurable and infinite. When integrated, it is neither singular nor dual. Arising once, it universally pervades the myriad nations;
it is neither slow nor swift, and it both accommodates and does not accommodate. It is neither ordinary nor sagely, neither wise nor foolish.
Only the person of non-mind and substance can unite with this void principle. For those who meet it, the obscure and dark is suddenly cleared away; for those who illumine it...
Luminosity is hazy; Vairocana is serene, neither increasing nor decreasing. The four modes of birth and the three realms of existence, upon hearing this, return to emptiness.
As for that which is profound, subtle, and silent—difficult to see and difficult to know—if one were to establish a single name or characteristic, it would neither join nor separate;
it is neither annihilated nor eternal, yet both extremes meet therein. It is without ignorance and without darkness; it is neither wisdom nor delusion. This is not of the mundane world.
This is what can be reached by the illumination of wise discernment; it is that which those possessing the wisdom of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) contemplate deeply.
This is the spontaneous realization of the empty mind, which is eternal life and non-extinction. To see while not seeing, it is without attachment and without dependence.
Among the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths in the world, none can reach this; it is solely the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma, the essential and excellent foundation. Since I—
Having heard this briefly, I could not remain silent. Embracing my ignorance and exhausting my wit, I have composed these humble words.

Although they do not penetrate the subtle principles, their general purport ultimately returns to spontaneity. My nature is muddled and deluded; I have written this to restrain myself and dispel my anxieties.
I pray that when the eminent and upright gentlemen see it, they will not laugh at me.

Chapter One: Clarifying that it is Neither Annihilated nor Eternal Do you not see that your own mind is neither annihilated nor eternal? It is universally present in all directions, yet does not enter into any direction.

Furthermore, it does not depend upon the limits of the past or the future. Moreover, it is neither round, nor short, nor long. It is profoundly still, without arising and without ceasing. It is not white...
It is not black; it is neither blue nor yellow. Although one contemplates and cognizes all phenomena, in reality, one does not abide within the center of that contemplation.
Sentient beings enter it, yet there is nothing entered; though they apprehend the six sense objects, there is in fact no injury.

The wise understand this with clear discernment; therefore, he is called the King of the Dharma. Having personally awakened to and known this dharma of non-cognition, his wisdom thereby becomes equal [to the Dharma].
Vajra, without relying on external conditions to support the inner treasury, the categories of precept, concentration, and wisdom naturally guard themselves.

Abiding securely at the summit of the Samādhi of Universal Transcendence, the delusions of inverted thoughts are forever extinguished. Realizing that all afflictions accord with the nature of reality (*tathatā*), one designates this emptiness as the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
For the sake of the assembly, proclaim and expound the eternal teaching; such a wondrous principle has never before been revealed. [The path of] practice...

Difficult! The path is difficult; its subtlety and mystery are exceedingly hard to traverse. If one uses non-cognition to illuminate the dharma of cognition, one realizes before one’s very eyes that there is fundamentally no arising.
Chapter Two: Clarifying True Illumination as Non-Illumination.

Do you not see that true illumination is clarity itself, yet its nature is without illumination? Its universal discernment is vast and open, yet it is without evenness. Abiding peacefully in non-knowledge, one knows clearly through illumination;
one thoroughly realizes that this clear illumination is itself ignorance. With a single mind, one forever severs all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*);
thus, for the first time, one diligently practices non-practice. This single mind is neither mind nor one; being without one and without mind, activity does not arise. Consciousness—
The mind is itself the dharma of non-arising; there is no non-arising apart from the dharma of arising.

If one knows that the nature of all conditions is without origination, then one may follow the mind’s inversions as they run wild in every direction. Understanding that the empty mind is without obstruction, one need not labor over worldly discourse.
If one further desires to struggle with such discourse, one is merely blinded by greed and delusion. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Delight in..."

Through knowledge and vision, the five aggregates and the afflictions arise again. If one can maintain the primordial limit (*koṭi*) with a wise mind, one will spontaneously attain the Right Path, which is serene and level.

With a nature that is upright and a mind that is equanimous, there is no [fixed] "uprightness. It is merely for the sake of leading all sentient beings that one assumes this level uprightness. The path traveled is difficult.

The path is difficult; he dwells constantly amidst the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Nirvāṇa is profound and mysterious, yet it does not constitute mere quiescence. Although there is birth and death, he alone remains pure and at ease.
Chapter Three: Clarifying the Phenomenal Aspect and the Ultimate Reality of the Mind.
Do you not see that the characteristics of the mind are subtle, most wondrous, and refined? It is neither a product of volition, nor a condition, nor can it be named as form.
Though it remains tranquil and devoid of marks, it is the very spirit of both the ordinary person and the sage. This spirit has no shape yet is ever-responsive;
though ever-responsive, it truly has no shape. The nature of the mind neither comes nor goes; though thoughts and concerns flow and turn, they truly have no station. Rightly...

To realize this is the awakening to the true and eternal. At the Deer Park, he established the honored scriptures as skillful means. To deliver those with false views and deluded thoughts, he caused them to know nirvana and attain peace.
He extensively expounded upon bodhi and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), yet these two dharmas are merely sounds.

Having thoroughly understood the proper and improper applications of sound, the afflictions of the three poisons neither diminish nor increase. Furthermore, one realizes that the five aggregates are all...
Emptiness and stillness: through right wisdom and non-arising, one restrains the six sense-faculties; within these six sense-faculties, one turns back toward the cessation of thought.
This is precisely the true city of Nirvana. The path is difficult; this difficult path has no going forth and no returning. Greed and hatred do not reside within or without.
Nor does it definitively exist in between.
Chapter Four elucidates signlessness and empty fusion:
"Have you not seen that within the definitive dharma there is no definitiveness? Delusive inversion is itself bodhi. If the mind...

To differentiate the dharma of bodhi is to become confused again by that very differentiation. If one realizes this confusion is non-differentiation, then confusion and differentiation are themselves bodhi.
Differentiating bodhi is neither identical nor different; it is eternally of one essence and does not involve mutual exclusion.
Abiding in the true nature of the emptiness of self-nature, in that emptiness there is no emptiness to be grasped. This same-essence great compassion encompasses all things.
Thus we know that the True Dharma does not conflict with delusion; this very state of confusion and darkness is itself devoid of intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, one need not discuss whether things are equal or unequal. If one abandons worldly toil (*saṃsāra*), there is no other dharma; it is like pure flowers growing from the mud. The Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata has no separate location;
it pervades the three realms and the hells (*niraya*). Yet these three realms and the hells are fundamentally non-existent. Who, then, could perceive their subtle and wondrous nature?

One comes to know the narrow path; traveling this road is difficult. This difficulty is, in its very essence, *nirvāṇa*. When both the internal and external—body and mind—are entirely empty and still, where can inversion, greed, and hatred find rest?
Chapter Five: Clarifying that Ordinary Beings and Sages are Neither One Nor Two.
Have you not seen that the delusions of affliction are not one? Though they are not one, they are also not many.
If one can illuminate and know their fundamental limit (*mūlakoṭi*), this is the true body, Vairocana. Entering even into a single atom, there is no obstruction; there is no obstruction.
The essence is quiescent and pervades the entire Sahā world; the two paths of ordinary beings and sages are not two separate places. Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are always in harmony.
Although one forcibly establishes the name "harmony," it is simply this very ignorance and delusion that is the true Buddha. The profound emptiness of Prajñā is wisdom that is not wisdom.
By means of the absence of mind and thought, one subdues the hosts of Māras. Having already studied this with sincere heart, I have briefly drawn upon my own clumsy thoughts to compose this song.
"The Difficulty of the Road. The road is difficult, yet the nature of the mind is truly vast and spacious; craving and desire are fundamentally and eternally quiescent.
The wise may linger here at their ease.
Chapter Six: Clarifying the Punishment of the Mind and the Untainted Nature of the Heart.
Have you not seen how the wise seek the mind and do not seek the Buddha? The cessation of all phenomena is itself free from greed and lust.
Greed and lust arise from the mind; therefore, I likewise punish the mind within the non-mind. If one seeks the mind and yet finds it not, it is naturally so.
There is no place where lust arises; lust neither arises nor ceases. Perversion is neither shallow nor deep, and yet it cannot be found as non-lustful desire.
There is neither attainment nor non-attainment—this wondrous state is difficult to seek; within the nature of the three poisons, it is always thus.
Fully endowed with constancy, they dwell in the forest of firmness. They take other matters of greed and lust as their Buddha-activity; the three poisons no longer intrude upon them at will.
Those who seek liberation yet sink back down, and through their discrimination of emergence and submergence, sink once more.

The Buddhas have skillfully mastered the three poisons; sentient beings, being deluded and false, cannot bear them. I, too, diligently cultivate the nature of the three poisons, and no longer pray for anything else.
The mind of all Buddhas: the path is difficult to traverse. Though the path is difficult, within the mind there is fundamentally nothing; this absence of things is pure bodhi.
Within a mind free from views, one constantly beholds the Buddha.

Chapter Seven: Clarifying the Non-contention of Prajñā Have you not seen that the true source of prajñā is fundamentally and eternally pure? The very root of birth and death is itself empty and subtle.
This birth and death is itself true prajñā; to seek it elsewhere apart from this is to act in contradiction. If the mind discriminates within birth and death, all sufferings [arise].
Poisonous afflictions pursue one another without end. If you now take worldly affairs as your craft, you will be unable to turn back from falsehood and delusion;
this is merely empty, provisional speech. Relying on neither of the two extremes of purity or impurity, one should mindlessly abandon the cycle of birth and death.
Nirvāṇa is mindless and does not pursue; nirvāṇa being mindless is itself saṃsāra. Saṃsāra being mindless is the radiance of prajñā.
When prajñā illuminates the mind, there is neither illumination nor function. Without illumination and without function, verbal expressions are severed, and one no longer desires to hold any views.
This is the Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Physician, who skillfully understands this medicine of mindlessness for the various diseases of the three realms of existence.
All can be healed. Traveling on difficult paths—though one sends them away again and again, recognize that this nature of sending is originally empty.
A mindless state is ultimately the Mahāyāna.
Chapter Eight: Clarifying that the Original Limit is Unattainable.
Do you not see that within the original limit there is no further "original"? Since there is no original, the true limit is unknown to anyone.

If a person, being without such [conceptual] knowledge, realizes this limit, it is pure, subtle, and wondrous, yet not to be considered extraordinary. Whether knowing or not knowing, it is always thus—regarding suffering and pleasure.
This is identical to great compassion. The sentient beings of the three realms are deluded and active; in its true record, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, even this unconditioned dharma does not exist. To forcibly give rise to a mind of one's own accord is weary suffering; all such weary suffering is empty, like a mirage or an echo.
Arising and ceasing without abiding, yet never separated; one who can know this mind is free from obstruction. Birth and death, though illusory, cannot bind them.
This single mind fully possesses all eighty-four thousand precepts and disciplines, yet it does not fall into the "superhuman states.
Though amidst steep precipices and extreme perils, it is not endangered. Among all phenomena, there is no phenomenon; yet worldly people remain in a state of frantic haste.
What do you wish to do? The journey is difficult. On this difficult path, there is nothing to be seen within the mind. In days past, one said that the Buddhas were far away;
now we know that greed and anger are themselves nirvāṇa.

Chapter Nine: Clarifying the Non-Interruption of Afflictions Do you not see that Mañjuśrī’s wondrous virtue is not far away? The three obstacles and the three poisons are themselves the three emptinesses.

The fivefold Dharma-body is enwrapped within the five aggregates. The six sense-bases, though lacking knowledge, constitute the six supernormal powers. How could the four inversions ever differ from the four fruits? The eight heterodoxies...

The eightfold noble path is identical in essence; the nature of the seven factors of enlightenment is no different. When the seven consciousnesses cease their wandering, they realize the True Doctrine;
all afflictions are then empty and quiescent. The Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas resides within the heart and mind, constantly followed by the patience of the Dharma.
We have drifted apart and do not meet; where do the Buddhas and Tathāgatas dwell? They are all within greed, lust, and desire.
Now I urge you to sever greed, lust, and desire—this is merely a skillful means to transform the ignorant. The fundamental nature of greed and desire is truly pure;
it is provisionally called "emptiness," yet even that name is empty. Traveling the road is difficult; this difficulty is not a mind within the mind. Entrusted.
Addressing the practitioner of true cultivation who is free from thought: Be careful not to discriminate against or disparage desire and lust.
Chapter Ten: Clarifying Quiescent Extinction and Mindlessness. Constantly Practice Diligence.
Do you not see that within the nature of quiescent extinction there is no extinction? Within true awakening there is no cognition; likewise, there is also nothing else.
There is non-cognition; it is pure, empty, and tranquil, free from spatial dimensions or rules. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus of itself, not brought about by causes.
Recollections and inverted thoughts are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) by nature. Even if one drifts throughout the three realms, within that mind there is truly no movement.
There is no going, no coming, and no abiding; one who skillfully realizes this non-abiding suffers no deficiency. The Buddhas, the Heroes of the World, are not merely "venerable and great."
The three poisons and the four inversions are not base; yet when one seeks them within the causal mind, nothing is found. Within the mind that lacks objects, conditions are nonetheless pervasive.
If you wish to swiftly seek the unsurpassed path, the nature of the three poisons can serve as a resource. The three poisons give rise to the three gates of liberation;
the seven consciousnesses further give rise to the seven factors of enlightenment. The inverted mind comes and goes without reality; its coming and going is without urgency.

Nor is there any delay. Awakening from all afflictions, one contemplates the objects before them; simply by chastising one’s own mind and turning it back, one realizes that the mind has no root—how could it have a foundation?
The six sense-objects and five desires cannot bind it. The path is difficult; yet this difficult path is subtle, wondrous, and most extraordinary.
In the past, with earnest diligence and vigor, one did not realize that such vigor was turning one's back on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Chapter Eleven: Clarifying the Sovereign Mastery in Attaining the Functions of the Dharmakāya Do you not see how the Great Being contemplates the dharmas within his own body? This body is the Tathāgata’s pure *dharmakāya*.
Like space, its coming and going are swift; it is uniquely liberated and sovereign, not dependent on others. It enters and exits the pores without obstruction. [Free from] craving and grasping...
While amidst the dust, one is not defiled by the dust; in the place of seeing, ordinary sentiments are equal to those of the sages. Apart from this, there is no other truth for seeking the Way.

Establishing all dharmas yet having no dharma—this is the unsurpassed reality of True Suchness (Tathatā). It has existed as the fundamental essence throughout billions of kalpas, yet it is not something produced anew.
Even now, seeing and awakening are not new. Having realized the Great Self, there is no self; being fully endowed with the Great Man, there is no person.
The holy body is beyond the description of ignorance; it is merely designated as "mind" through skillful means.
This very mind is the truly eternal Dharma, and it is also the supreme treasure of Nirvana. May all students of the Way awaken to this together, each guarding their own gate.

Yet the ford is barred; the journey is difficult. Though the names of these difficulties differ, their underlying principle is no different. If one can thoroughly understand that there is no birth-and-death, one will then be able to eliminate the clouds of birth-and-death.
Chapter Twelve: Clarifying the Vajra Liberation Have you not seen that vajra words are not merely conventional reality?
The myriad phenomena of the universe are one in emptiness. This emptiness, the non-substantiality, is the Mother of Buddhas;
it is also the supreme jewel of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Yet worldly people do not know to seek this treasure, and thus they remain in poverty.
In a daze, you are a slave to the six realms of existence; you do not serve the Dharmakāya Buddha within your own body. You dig holes looking outward to bow before stupas;
at first glance, this may seem like diligent practice, but when scrutinized, everything within your being is coarse. You employ such a coarse mind merely to flaunt your words.
Failing to comprehend the true source, one is thus deluded; following emotional recollections and thoughts, one engages in discrimination.

The five aggregates and six thieves compete to slaughter [the mind]; one refuses to seek the unsurpassed Way. Knowing only the false while seeking fame and reputation, though the mouth proclaims goodness, evil still arises.
Empty words claiming reality instead turn into falsehood; I now reverse the false and hold it as real, yet I do not realize the truth.
Entering the state of nirvana without remainder is a difficult path; this difficult path is entirely illusory throughout the world. The nature of the ten fetters and the five aggregates is ignorance;
therein, fools create their own obstructions.
Chapter Thirteen: Clarifying Quiescence—Neither Illumination nor Attainment.
Do you not see that all phenomena are merely provisional designations within emptiness? Quiescence has no gate, yet it serves as the gateway to the Dharma.
Among all phenomena, the mind is sovereign. Now I no longer seek the source of the mind. Having thoroughly investigated the source of the mind and found it not, how could one know [anything else]?
All phenomena are fundamentally without root; using this rootless mind to illuminate objects, the illumination becomes increasingly obscure.
When this very obscured mind attempts to illuminate itself, the principle of correct illumination never truly exists. Thus, both the illumination and the object remain distinct and different.
Therefore, the wise cannot discourse upon it; worldly people, in their madness, insist on making distinctions. Within the void, they perceive only the chaotic spirit.

If one can use wisdom to illuminate so that there is no illumination, then the intellect that discriminates and illuminates will cease its flight. All phenomena are fundamentally thus—who created them?
They are quiescent, yet there is neither stillness nor clamor. Thus we know that the inverted perceptions of sentient beings are themselves but sentient beings.
O Unsurpassed Honored One, the road is difficult to travel. Though the road is difficult, one abandons delusion only to fall back into it again.
While I am able to subdue birds and beasts, this single thief of the mind alone is difficult to tame.

Chapter Fourteen: Clarifying the Three Emptinesses and the Absence of Self-Nature Have you not seen that the minds of the Buddhas and sages are unimpeded? To open the way for transformation, they speak of the three absences. Yet, though they speak of the three absences, in reality they do not speak;
for the mind does not abide within the myriad objects of experience. Even if one were to commit the five heinous crimes through inverted views, it would follow from their own deluded sentiments.

All that is done returns to suchness; one embraces the fundamental purity (*pǔbó*) and clarifies the spirit by contemplating non-contemplation. Furthermore, one does not differentiate or strive to extinguish all traces.

Thus, one settles the mind without selecting a particular place, for one clearly knows that the essence of the ultimate and the conventional is not distinct. One quiets discursive thought so that the mind is empty, yet does not abandon worldly affairs.
When names, principles, words, and deeds do not support one another, and the mind wavers without relying on the six sense objects;

when it follows the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and accords with emptiness and voidness—neither going nor coming, never abiding; when the mental spirit is utterly exhausted yet not non-existent; when the body is not destroyed and one accords with the single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*);
when one does not sever desire and lust yet is not bound by them—if one claims there is no difference, one binds oneself; to say their substance is different...
The turning of the body is like a dream or an illusion, devoid of reality; since it was originally non-existent, how could it be removed? The path is difficult;
this difficult path is suddenly hard to manage. Ordinary beings see through deluded views with their distinctions, but in true concentration there is neither self nor other.

Chapter Fifteen: Clarifying that Emptiness and Existence Are Not Contradictory Do you not see that false views are neither extremes nor separate from extremes? Erroneous conceptualization is likewise not an objective condition. One’s own mind is neither mind nor mental activity;
it constantly comes and goes, yet in reality there is no transition. It is like a vajra, difficult to destroy; [this is the state of] all Buddhas.
Using this, one makes the gold firm. The world praises the wondrousness of Nirvana; my Way regards birth and death as most profound and mysterious.
This is the supreme patience (*kṣānti*) regarding non-arising, and it is also the Mahā-unimpeded Dhyāna. The true person contemplates thus by means of the mind.
Not led astray by the eight winds, one enjoys celestial bliss with a mind free from attachment. How could trivial wealth or beauty ever entangle such a person?
Whether encountering suffering or joy, the mind remains unchanging; forever parting from discursive thoughts, one forgets the torment of anxiety.

With an empty mind, devoid of "person" or "mine," one follows nature’s flow, appearing as if dazed. In reality, one perceives that the constant Dharma has no fixed nature, knowing that all phenomena lack intrinsic self-nature.
He is titled "The Wise One. Traveling the road is difficult. This difficulty is neither empty nor existent. Both existence and non-existence are simultaneously dispelled and simultaneously preserved.
When both are preserved, there is neither dispelling nor receiving.

Chapter Sixteen: Clarifying the Maras and Enemies Have you not seen that the Great Way is tranquil and still, beyond thought or seeking? It permeates and unifies all phenomena, which are all profoundly deep.

All things are serene, without arising or ceasing; inverted discrimination arises entirely from the mind. When the wise seek the mind, they find no location; they are left in a state of vast, open bewilderment.
The marks of form are free from lust; what is seen is clear and distinct. It is like a person with diseased eyes seeing needles in the air.
If one understands in person that these are inverted perceptions, one will not be drifted away or submerged by false suffering. All phenomena in the world are like a mirage.
The practitioner should be careful not to harbor resentment or aversion; always use the empty mind to reflect inwardly. One can thus bear even the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.

The journey is difficult; yet this difficult path is subtle and wondrous, truly without peer. If one realizes that the six sense-faculties are empty and non-existent, the various demons and the thieves of the fetters will naturally submit.
Chapter Seventeen: Clarifying the Function of the Equality of Dharma-nature.
Do you not see that the dharma-nature is without cognition and is ineffable? Whether tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), all are equally void and pervasive.

Although they diverge and manifest as the various stages (*bhūmi*), if one seeks their fundamental limit, they are entirely identical. Furthermore, there is no dharma of "sameness" that can be made identical, nor is there any [duality] to be negated.
Taking emptiness as the means to realize emptiness—if you wish to know this sublime and wondrous path, simply exhaustively investigate the thicket of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
As it truly is, there is neither coming nor going, nor is it definitively located within the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*); this is precisely the sourceless, true *dharmadhātu*.
Serene and eternally abiding, it has neither beginning nor end. How difficult is the journey! How difficult is the road—how can suffering and joy ever come to an end?
At times he goes to the West to the Land of Immeasurable Life; at other times he manifests through transformation in the East.
Chapter Eighteen: Clarifying the Inconceivable Buddha-Mother.
Have you not seen that love, desire, and lust are the mothers of all Buddhas? The World-Honored Buddhas have craving and desire as their children. Since time immemorial, Bodhi has been my craftsman;
now he makes me the master craftsman for the multitude. In the past, I sought the Buddha through a thousand external means, yet the Buddha was [already] within.
Only now, within my robes, do I realize that the immeasurable deluded mind is fundamentally the Way; that the three poisons and four inversions are inconceivable;

and that practicing compassion toward the manifold sufferings of the unreal is itself ignorance of the fact that all such sufferings are compassion—that hatred and ignorance are most subtle and wondrous.
The wise cannot conceive of this. In the past, one toiled diligently to study knowledge and views, yet one did not know that knowledge and views are themselves devoid of knowing.

The four realms of existence and the three miserable paths do not truly exist; the three obscurations and the three liberations are inseparable. The path is difficult to traverse, yet on this difficult path there is nothing to be grasped or forgotten.
To fully realize that afflictions are without the notion of arising—this is the Tathāgata sitting at the site of enlightenment.
Chapter Nineteen: Clarifying Effort Without Discernment Do you not see the sons of the Buddhas with upright minds? Because they perceive that there is no mind, they do not grieve.

Knowing that the mind is not the mind and that thought is not thought, how could they harbor sorrow when the eight winds of worldly fortune assail them? Moving east and west with the winds, they have no sense of "mine"; they are uniquely liberated and carefree.
Do not moor the boat. Even if it should remain still, it is ultimately not abiding; though it travels throughout the ten directions, it does not flow away.
When one does not perceive a self, one dwells in non-self. How excellent! To follow one’s nature, letting it sink or float as it may.

The delusions of the world possess no reality; what, then, is there for me to seek within this? Simply employ a non-mind to awaken to non-awakening, and likewise practice correctly within non-practice. If...
People do not realize this state; they should not merely assume the name of a bhikṣu. They become slaves to their own deluded minds, bound by the fetters of craving and lacking freedom.
Thus, their various sufferings and afflictions increase further, and for eternal kalpas they remain long-term prisoners within the three realms.
Life and death are linked together, becoming ever more intense; it is judged that they can never attain lasting rest. The path is difficult. The path is difficult.
Do not allow thoughts to pass beyond one another; the thought of no-thought is the true. True thought has no reality, yet it returns to its own radiance.
Chapter Twenty: Clarifying the Subtle and Wondrous Lord.
Have you not seen that unsurpassed Bodhi is most near? The four elements and five aggregates are all profoundly deep; in their essence, they are pure.
Pure and wondrous, it is difficult to know. Failing to awaken to this mind is truly violent and reckless. Within the nature of harmony, there is no substantial reality;

therefore, it is called the essential core of all dharmas. Within it, there is neither delusion nor truth; one simply employs the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as the subtle and wondrous. When seeking its essence, which is quiescent, it should not be described in words.
Names and titles are provisionally established for the sake of sentient beings; if one knows that names and titles are not themselves names, [one realizes the truth].
Understanding sentient beings, one knows the Buddha’s teaching; awakening to the true cause that is without [inherent] cause, one shall attain that which is without cause and without retribution.
Skillfully penetrating craving, one attains the unborn; ignorance is without movement in its coming and going. One does not see the holy fruit as distinct from ordinary sentiment;
to differentiate between the holy and the ordinary is itself inverted. If a person has no aspiration and no cultivation, they will certainly become [a Buddha].
The Guide of the World traverses a difficult path; this difficult path is neither defiled nor pure. Both affirmation and negation are extinguished, yet they remain present.

In the fifteen verses on the ease of the path, Buddha and emptiness are of one essence. Emptiness and Buddha have always been identical; everything encountered by the eye is thus. Within the self-nature of no-mind, all is as it is.
The path of practice is easy; it is not that one does not practice. When the mind is eternally stilled, this very state is non-arising.
Sentient beings are the Buddhas; the Buddhas are the elders of sentient beings. The Three Jewels are never separate; enlightenment is shared by all.
The path of practice is easy; ease is truly non-action. Hold the sutra without moving the mouth; sit in meditation while lying down all day long.
There is no birth and no location; where there is no location, that is non-birth. If you seek a place of non-birth, non-birth will not arise from such a place.
The path of practice is easy; the path of Luoyu is broad and level. With no-mind comes true liberation; one’s own nature is free to move in all directions.
Bodhi has no location; where there is no location, that is bodhi. If you seek a place for bodhi, you will remain deluded throughout this life and for many kalpas.
The path of practice is easy; this ease is truly not in vain. Without discriminating between good and evil, this is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).

Both existence and non-existence are liberation; the cessation of conditioned breaths resides in the unborn (*anutpāda*). Awakening (*bodhi*) is a delusion; birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is the most essential.
The path of practice is easy; those on the path need have no doubts. Understand my words in this way: to cultivate the Way, one need not rely on a teacher.
The Eastern Mountain floats upon the water; the Western Mountain moves without staying still. Beneath the Northern Dipper lies Jambudvīpa—this is the place of true liberation.
The road is easy to travel, yet people do not recognize it. At midnight, the sun shines bright; failing to awaken to this truth, one’s exhaustion is extreme.
A fierce wind does not move the trees; beating a drum, no sound is heard. When the sun rises, the trees cast no shadows; an ox walks upon the surface of the water.
The path of practice is easy. Luoyu is truly pitiable. Cultivating the Way, one understands this meaning: stretch out both legs and sleep.
The Buddha-mind and the minds of sentient beings—these three never shift. Emptiness accords with ultimate truth; self and others abide in non-action.
Traveling on the road is easy; traveling on the road is truly difficult to fathom. I send this message to those who travel: you must surely exert great effort.
Others say that traveling on the road is difficult; I say that traveling on the road is easy. Having entered the mountains twelve years ago, I stretch out my two legs and sleep.
The path of practice is easy; do not engage in discursive thought. With a mind of non-duality in each instant, all day long is heaven.
Sumeru is the father of the mustard seed, and the mustard seed is the grandfather of Sumeru. Mountains and seas become level ground; one burns ice to brew tea.
The path of practice is easy. The path of practice is truly profound and mysterious. The bodhicitta resides within it, yet worldly people do not perceive it at all.
Existence and non-existence, coming and going—the mind is forever stilled. Within, without, and in between—the mind is entirely absent.

If you wish to seek the true abode of the Tathāgata Buddha, simply look at the stone ox giving birth to a young elephant. The path of practice is easy. The path of practice must be undertaken early. There is no need to study much.
I have heard: "Speechlessness is the true Way;
non-action is the absence of doing; the absence of doing is the absence of mind. Where there is neither seeing nor mind, willow flowers sink to the bottom of the water."
The path of practice is easy; ease is truly non-attainment. To expound thousands of varieties of treatises is not as good as a moment of silence.
The insentient is precisely the Way; wood and stone are entirely *tathatā*. When one realizes this, the entire environment is it; if one does not awaken, one remains forever alienated and distant.
The path of practice is easy; this ease is truly delightful. One attains perfect enlightenment in a single instant, without needing to don the three teachings.
To have nothing is true non-action; true non-action is known by few. Non-being has no location; that which has no location is non-being.
The path of practice is easy; let those on the path not be startled. There is no such thing as "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) reality;
there is only the empty name "unconditioned. Without self and without person is true renunciation; what need is there to shave the head or dye the robes?

If you wish to recognize the true liberation of carefree wandering, simply look at the water buffalo growing elephant tusks. The path of practice is easy; you who travel the path, listen attentively! No awakening, no bodhi.
Ti. Neither defilement nor purity.
The sixth chapter, Chapter One:
Praising the long-standing yearning for the pearl, yet not having obtained it to this day.

Today is the day you bring forth illumination; response and resonance lie in the clarity of the Yang. Your contemplation is profound and exhaustive; your steadfast resolve is truly difficult to equal.
Remembering you in the morning brings longing; gazing toward you at evening moves my heart with grief. If we meet beneath the sacred tree, may our deliverance never be forgotten.

Those with evil views are solitary and withered; may we all together hasten toward the resplendent path. Flying as a pair to the summit of the white sun, our breath emits the radiance of purple clouds.
Divine dragons attend to the left and right of the Brahma realm; scattered flowers arrive in fragrant abundance. In this lush and ever-blissful state, we ascend majestically to the Golden Hall.
Chapter Two: Praising the Severance of Bonds and Fulfilling Former Aspirations In recent years, did you not turn your back on the celestial palaces?
Reflecting on suffering, you have been temporarily bound here. Now that the golden embrace has been relaxed, the flowing black robes have become mutual acquaintances.

Relying solely on mutual virtuous companionship, we follow one another; depending on this guidance, we forget our weariness. Together we ascend to the realm of the eight stages, and together we delight in the jeweled lotus ponds.
With bodies of refined gold, we bring to fruition the wondrous fruits of all manner of marvels.

Polishing the bright pearl until it is lustrous, its radiance shines forth so that all may see.

Exhortatory Verses, Three:

One directly transcends the ocean of the three realms of existence and proceeds straight to the path of the *sākyamuni*. Meeting both the equal and the unequaled, one realizes together that which is both constrained and unconstrained.
Breaking the precepts is like a leaking boat; one sinks into the great rivers and oceans. Only when facing utter despair does one call upon the Buddha, yet one’s resolve remains unaltered.
