Amidst the mountain valleys and forests, the land abounded in *bōxīng* (Cinnamomum camphora) trees; consequently, it was named Mount Xiangshan.

The Dharma Master resided there for a long time, yet no one knew of his presence. Later, a woodcutter encountered him; his physical form appeared extremely withered, yet his spirit was vibrant and refined as he sat alone beneath a great tree.
The man approached and spoke with him, finding him most pleasing. The Dharma Master said to him, "This place is fit for the construction [of a monastery]."
"I regret only that my strength is insufficient and I cannot reach it myself. The woodcutter then requested that the Dharma Master leave the mountain to receive offerings at the home of a layperson.
The Dharma Master said, "If there is a place where the five pungent vegetables are not grown, I shall go there. The woodcutter reflected upon this.
There was one family that, from previous generations, had never planted this [fruit]. He then took the Dharma Master to their home.
Thereupon, the people of the village and hamlet vied with one another to provide offerings.

He led them by the hand toward their dwelling place and drove four pieces of wood into the ground as markers, saying, "This is where a temple may be established. Later, he traveled for a short time to the south of Songqiaoshan.

He encountered Lou Yan, an attendant of the Liang court. Lou Yan also possessed discerning insight; seeing that the Dharma Master’s features were exceptionally refined and extraordinary, he knew him to be no ordinary man.
He engaged him in conversation and was greatly pleased. The Dharma Master said to him, "I am a humble monk from a foreign land who has come here practicing *dhūta*.
I share a profound karmic affinity with you, my patron (*dānapati*), from past lives. Now I wish to propagate the Buddha's work together with you, serving as a vessel to ferry across the multitudes."
Daosheng then made an appointment with Huiyan to meet at the pine grove where he resided in the eighth month of the following year.
At that time, the Buddha-dharma was still in its infancy, and Huiyan did not yet understand what Daosheng intended; furthermore, he suspected that Daosheng might be a sage.

Therefore, when the appointed time arrived, he cleared away the brambles and thorns, opening a path for twenty *li* until he finally reached the Dharma Master’s location, where he saw the Dharma Master wearing...
Wearing robes of discarded rags, he sat in the full-lotus posture and joyfully said to Yan: "The Way of Bodhi brings benefit on a vast scale.
We should together, as a donor and a recipient, honor and establish the Triple Gem and wash away the six sense-objects.

If we once lose our correct retribution, we shall not regain a human body for kalpas on end; how can one expect a blind turtle to encounter the hole of a floating yoke again? Upon hearing these words, Yan then accompanied him.
Together they resolved to cultivate the Bodhi-mind and to honor and propagate the True Dharma.

The Dharma Master, together with Yan and the others, surveyed the terrain and saw that a thousand crags rose majestically, encircling the site from all four directions. Consequently, the place where the four stakes had been driven in was named "The Flank of the Dragon" (Longye).
They then jointly established a vihāra, naming it Xiangshan Temple. Furthermore, they constructed a small storehouse beside it for storage.
It could hold about one *shu* of rice and was very plain and crude in appearance.

The Dharma Master ordered that one *shu* of rice be purchased to fill it, taking from this grain daily to provide for the monks and to give to the poor. As the supply neared exhaustion, people would immediately bring more;
it never became empty. At that time, people called it the "Ever-Full Granary. Later, some people found the granary too small and enlarged it further. Furthermore—
After the completion of the carvings and decorations, for an entire year no one provided him with rice; his granary remains there to this day.
At that time, many believers from the villages and hamlets donated their rice paddies to provide for the practitioners from the four quarters.
Later, several dozen mountain bandits, all carrying weapons, came to plunder his wealth; however, the Dharma Master simply sat peacefully in his quiet room.
He felt no fear. Since the thieves were unable to enter, they merely raised their voices and reviled him, ordering the monk to come out quickly.
The Dharma Master calmly said to them from within his room, "My appearance is unseemly; I am unfit to meet with you, O donors. After a short while...

The hands and feet of the bandits were all unable to move, as if they had been bound by others; consequently, they fell to the ground, their spirits shattered and in utter confusion, no longer recognizing one another.
The leader of the bandits was struck with terror and apologized for his crimes. Only after a long while did they regain consciousness. At that time...
The officials and commoners of the district declared that this rebel was a great pest and bound him together with others to hand him over to the Prefectural Governor.

The rebel’s followers ordered his mother not to enter the mountains, and she went to the Dharma Master’s location to request [his intervention]. The Dharma Master spoke to her only in gentle words, saying, “Do not worry too much;
you shall soon be released. On the eighth day of the fourth month, she was indeed pardoned and released. At that time, the monastery collectively constructed a sacred shrine and established...

During an Unrestricted Dharma Assembly (*paśca-bhikṣu-pūjā*), ten thousand people from both the monastic and lay communities were together pulling on a hemp rope to raise a banner. Suddenly, the rope snapped in the middle;
those pulling it all fell down in disarray, not knowing what to do. The Dharma Master then gave rise to this thought: "What demonic interference has caused this?
He then took a silver flask from his person, poured water into his alms bowl, and suddenly, with great compassion, grasped it from both inside and out.
He wept. After a short while, he recited incantations and prostrated. When the prostrations were finished, he smiled joyfully and immediately took up his bowl and circumambulated the stupa once.
The stupa then stood firm on its own, without requiring human labor. At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Huikai who took leave for a brief visit home.
His mother had secretly prepared a chicken for him; thinking no one would know, Huikai ate it privately with his mother. When morning came...
He was returning to the mountain, which the Dharma Master perceived through his supernormal knowledge; he therefore rebuked him.

Furthermore, there was a man who sold vegetables and fruits in the market to provide for a vegetarian offering. Encountering a time when the host was away, he secretly took a small amount of ginger and returned it to prepare for the offering.
When the midday meal arrived and the monks were all seated, the host served the food in order. The Dharma Master accepted all the items, yet alone—
He took some ginger. The master then said to him, "To take what was not permitted—why do you engage in such unauthorized theft? The host merely stood there, shrinking with shame.
On the third day of the fifth month of the first year of the Putong era, County Magistrate Xiao Zimù was about to go to the temple to pay his respects to the Dharma Master.

He first passed through the villages and accepted offerings of wine and food from the common people; only after becoming drunk and satiated did he enter the temple. The Dharma Master had closed his room.

He did not come out; he merely sent word, saying, "The Magistrate must return quickly. Magistrate Xiao’s expression suddenly turned stern; he felt like setting fire to the temple but did not do so. He then intended to advance a little further, but after a long while he could not proceed. He finally returned to the county seat. The next day, lay devotees from near the temple came to ask the Dharma Master, "Yesterday the Magistrate paid his respects; why did he not go forward? The Dharma Master replied: [The Dharma Master replied: "The Magistrate was about to enter the temple when he saw a monk sitting cross-legged on a stone pillar, reciting the *Heart Sūtra*. The Magistrate asked, 'Who is this? The monk said, 'I am a guest-monk from the capital. The Magistrate then asked, 'What sūtras does this guest-monk recite? The monk replied, 'I recite the *Heart Sūtra*.

The Magistrate said, 'Recite it for me. The monk then recited it for him. When the Magistrate heard the sound of the *Heart Sūtra*, he felt as though he were ascending to heaven. He then bowed to the monk and departed. Upon returning, he thought to himself, 'This is truly a holy place; I cannot enter here. Thus, he did not go forward. The lay devotees said, "The Magistrate is indeed a man of great virtue. The Magistrate subsequently built a monastery there and named it the "Monastery of the Heart Sūtra. It remains to this day. This is the origin of the name of that monastery. The Magistrate later became the Governor of Guangzhou. He died at the age of sixty-eight. His son, the Magistrate of Shanyang, also died at the age of fifty-nine. Both were men of great virtue. Their deaths occurred because they had failed to repay their karmic debts. This is what is called the power of the *Heart Sūtra*. One should know that its efficacy is inconceivable. If one recites it with a sincere heart, one will surely attain liberation. One should not harbor doubts. If one harbors doubts, one will receive no benefit. Therefore, one should believe and accept it with all one's heart. Do not be negligent. If you practice this diligently, you will surely attain the Way. This is the true teaching of the Buddha. You should take it to heart and propagate it widely. Do not let it perish. This is my exhortation to you. May you all attain peace and happiness. Amens. "Why does the Master not come out? He replied, "I am passing by for recreation; this is why I do not come out.
You have resolved to set fire to the temple, and that is why you, Excellency, do not proceed. He continued, "In the future, this region shall suffer a great drought for thirty years.

The Attendant Lou Yan hurriedly reported these words to the Magistrate Xiao, who was greatly terrified. He immediately galloped to the temple and, with profound sincerity, paid his respects and made a formal request.
He repented. The Master then explained the wondrous path of Bodhi to him. Xiao Lingyu received the teaching with joy and departed.
On the fourteenth day of the third month of that year, the Dharma Master went to attend a vegetarian feast in a nearby village and refused to return to the mountain.

The assembly earnestly entreated the Master, but he vowed not to look back toward the north. He then said: "I have come here through the convergence of conditions; when my conditions are exhausted, I shall depart."
They departed. Thereupon, the men and women, filled with grief and longing, wept as they followed one after another along the road. On that day, the Dharma Master suddenly set out toward the south.
Looking up at the southern mountains, he saw purple clouds covering their peaks, whereupon he said joyfully, "This is a place where a monastery may be established."

He traveled to another mountain where the river was overflowing its banks. The boatmen refused to ferry him across, so the Master spread his parasol upon the water, grasped an iron fish-shaped bell in his hand, and crossed by cutting through the current.
He proceeded south to Jieting Tangxia, where he saw the Great Being (Mahāsattva) wading through the water seeking fish;
thereupon, he revealed the miraculous traces of the Great Being’s divine power and pointed out the place where he had practiced the Way before departing. He continued on his journey.
Upon reaching Mount Lai, he stopped at the place where purple clouds gathered and established a vihāra on its summit, naming it Laishan Temple.
The Dharma Master often said to others, "Mount Lai will be sovereign for a short time; Mount Xiang will be long-lasting but not sovereign."
From this time forth, the donors of faith to this monastery have been so abundant that its wealth and provisions are plentiful;

the monks who arrive in succession are provided for according to their needs, even for many decades beyond. Since the site is situated among forests and hills, there are occasionally spirits and supernatural beings there.
The former residents were deeply unsettled; they gradually departed until the site fell into ruin.
Later, the elders of the neighboring villages collectively moved the temple’s nameplate and established it ten *li* due north, in a level valley where they could live in peace.

Xiangshan, however, remained with a population of moderate wealth and poverty, remaining as it was from the beginning even to this day. Furthermore, the Dharma Master planted many varieties of fruit trees on the southern mountain of the monastery.
The tree. Every morning and evening, he personally walked along the path and encountered the Great Being (Mahāsattva) there;

greatly delighted, he rubbed the Great Being’s head and said, "I reflect that I am about to journey westward, and thus shall not meet with the flourishing of the Bodhisattva’s Way. Thereupon, they each returned to their respective dwellings.
After the Dharma Master had been at the temple for several days, he remained to stay at the Iron Fish-Bell (Tieyu-qing). As for this Iron Fish-Bell, it was made of iron...
He fashioned it into a shape resembling a fish. This temple has struck it every morning and evening until the present day.
When the Dharma Master traveled west to the foot of the Southern Mountain within the borders of Jinhua County, he said, "This is also a suitable place to establish a monastery.

He then pierced the ground with his staff and said, "At this spot, a well may be dug. Subsequently, a monastery was indeed established on that site as Longpan Monastery, and a well was excavated at the place where the staff had pierced the earth.
The well was not very deep; even during periods of extreme drought, it did not run dry.

The Master then traveled westward to the borders of Longqiu, where he gazed upon the southern mountains whose rocky formations were solitary and magnificent. He remarked, "This place is also fit for establishing a monastery.
Consequently, he took up residence there and constructed an araṇya. Later, this was named Longqiu Rock Monastery. After the monastery was completed, the Master proceeded further west.
He traveled on and entered the Wanshan (Ten Thousand Virtues) Mountain Pass. Seeing that the mountain’s winding and coiled terrain was suitable, he wished to establish a vihāra there.
Suddenly, he encountered three donors, to whom he pointed out the location. The three men then made a vow together, saying, "We shall provide you with provisions."
To encourage the fulfillment of this meritorious deed, the Dharma Master asked, "How far is the donor's residence from here?
They replied, "Neither near nor far; he is merely the local landowner of this region. Thereupon, each identified their own surname: one said Chen, one said Zhao, and one said Su;
none, however, mentioned their personal names. When the vihāra was nearly completed, it was named Li Liu (Leaving the Six).
At Chen Temple, the three men then took their leave of one another and departed; it was unknown where they ultimately went.
The Dharma Master then traveled westward to Mount Mengdu. This mountain had previously been home to white deer, and the sound of bells and chimes was often heard there.
He further established a vihāra at this site, naming it Sancang Temple. Thus began the Dharma Master’s journey from his departure at Xiangshan Temple until this point.
In total there were seven locations, all possessing the finest geomantic advantages of mountains and rivers; offerings from both monastics and laypeople continue to this day.
When the Tripitaka Master’s work was completed, the Dharma Master returned to Longqiu Rock Temple. As he approached his passing, the Great Being knew it in his own mind and said to his disciples:
"Master Sengsong has already returned to the capital and awaits me in the Heavenly Palace. I shall go there together with him to deliver sentient beings."
Those people have already passed away completely.
The Dharma Master and Ācārya Huiji was of the Wang secular clan, named Shezhi. He was a native of Dakuo Village in Youxiang, Fuchun County, Wu Commandery. His family was originally...

He was poor and lowly, and always had creditors who pursued him. At that time, he was subject to corvée labor in the various districts and counties; fearing he would be summoned and arrested, he fled.
He fled to Mount Tiantai, shaved his head to become a monk, and practiced the ascetic dhūta austerities with diligent devotion to the Buddha-dharma.

Having avoided official affairs, he did not remain in one fixed location. Hearing that there was a Great Being (Mahāsattva) in Dongyang who had a profound understanding of the Mahāyāna, he set out for the Shuanglin Monastery by night.
Since he did not know the exact location, he proceeded by following his natural momentum. Whenever he reached a crossroads, he would focus his mind single-pointedly.
He closed his eyes and followed the direction he had been given until he reached the path leading directly to the Great Being’s abode.

Previously, the Great Being had said, "I shall relinquish my wealth and treasures to establish a Dharma assembly for the sake of sentient beings suffering within the three realms. Thereafter, his heart was slightly troubled.
That very night, he saw Śākyamuni Buddha in a dream, who consoled him, saying, "Do not be distressed. I shall dispatch a śramaṇa..."
A gatekeeper came to assist you. Furthermore, during the night, in a dream, a small boy was born from your mouth;
he lay supine upon my knees and gazed intently at my face. I asked the boy, "Do you recognize me? He replied, "Why would I not recognize you? You are Maitreya Buddha.
When the boy fell to the ground, he immediately became a virtuous śramaṇa. Three days after I awoke, the Dharma Master arrived.
The Great Being bestowed upon him the Dharma-gate of explanation, whereupon he attained clear and profound awakening.

At that time, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty was widely recruiting men of outstanding talent, who gathered from all quarters like clouds; yet the Great Being of the Double Grove (Śālavatī) had not yet been invited.

The Great Being spoke leisurely to the Dharma Master, saying: "If you, Venerable One, are able to cultivate the untainted noble path, you should go to the kingdom on my behalf and offer up your head."

They mutually testified to this, vowing to bring about liberation. Thereupon, the Dharma Master relied upon the Great Being (Mahāsattva) as his disciple for ascetic practice and resolved to generate the Bodhicitta.

He propagated and expounded the True Dharma, not begrudging even his own body or life. He then sought an audience with the King to personally recount the Great Being’s vows and practices for delivering sentient beings.
Upon arriving at the capital, the Dharma Master pressed forward and personally proclaimed the virtues of the Great Being.
Because he had been rebuked for his work, he sought to clear his own name and was thus acquitted. He then proceeded to the palace gate, where he struck the drum to present his case.
He was sentenced to labor at the Department of Coinage for one year. During his time in service, he converted others and constructed several stories of a brick stupa.

The supervisor, impressed by his courageous diligence, petitioned for his release. Subsequently, he returned to the mountains; both monastics and laypeople regarded this Great Being as a manifestation of the White [Avalokiteśvara].
There were many among the disciples of the śramaṇas who gave rise to doubts and engaged in slander.
The Dharma Master, together with the layman Zhuan Pumin, deliberated before the Three Jewels and made a vow, saying:

"If the Way and Dharma of the Great Being are not propagated, we shall each undergo ascetic practices to spread the True Path. Thereupon, Pumin cut off his nose and burned his fingers, widely performing acts of devotion for the Buddha.
He continued his journey to the county magistrate, Xiao Xu. As he propagated the Way and spread the teachings, Tanpumin said, "I truly practice the Dharma with my whole heart.
His attendants asked, "Your heart is within; how can it be seen? Tanpumin immediately went outside to borrow a knife and cut off one of his ears to manifest his resolve.
Magistrate Xiao and his attendants praised him. A former Great Being once said to people, "Huiji is..."
Avalokiteśvara universally pities this Mañjuśrī; thus they mutually testify to one another that it would not have been possible to sacrifice one's hair and skin were it not for this [power].

From then on, the Dharma Master practiced giving, released living beings, rescued those in suffering, and treated illnesses as he traveled through the provinces and kingdoms, never complaining of hardship or fatigue.
Singing of immeasurable joy, he spoke this verse: "The Great Being has come from Tuṣita, causing the earth to tremble."
He traveled through various lands where lotuses grew covering the ground. He was specially permitted to welcome Maitreya; when Puguang first began his practice of the Way, boundless worlds shook.
Heaven turned back and the earth rotated again, all merging into a single pore. At that time, among those in the human world who chanted this verse, most did not understand it.
However, some who grasped its principle remarked that since the Great Being was already a portion of Maitreya Buddha.

The Master’s body was [an emanation]. Furthermore, the Dharma Master served as an incarnation of Avalokiteśvara. A sutra states: "When Maitreya descends to be born, flowers will rain down, covering the earth;
only when Avalokiteśvara attains enlightenment will he become the Tathāgata Samantaprabha. The verse says, "Shaking all lands," which refers to the time of Maitreya’s descent.
"Turning heaven and overturning earth" refers to the traces of Avalokiteśvara’s responsive transformations. The Dharma Master constantly arrived at...
At Longhua Monastery in Kuaiji, [the Master] saw a limping man arrive leaning on two staffs, who said, "I have been ill for forty years;

I beg you to treat me. The Dharma Master said, "Simply focus your mind on me with single-mindedness. The limping man followed his instructions. After a short while, the Dharma Master told him to let go of one staff;
the limping man did so. Next, he told him to let go of the other staff; the limping man did so and then brushed off his robes and departed. The limping man remained there in reliance upon the Master.
He was then able to run about. Later, while in the marketplace, the Dharma Master saw an old man suffering from deafness who said, "I have been like this for several years;
even skilled physicians could not cure me. The Dharma Master also said, "Call upon my name with single-minded devotion. Once he had finished speaking, he had someone call out to the man.
The deaf man heard slightly at first, but after being called three times, his hearing was completely restored. He then departed. Upon reaching Taimo County, there was a man named Jingjin Dao.
There was a man whose mind was afflicted by a chronic knot-like ailment, and another monk who had long suffered from white leprosy;

both monks came to seek treatment, and the Dharma Master again instructed each of them to single-mindedly recite his name, whereupon they were both healed. Furthermore, at Xin'an County, he encountered a bhikṣuṇī who had been suffering from epilepsy for many years;
she also came to seek treatment, and the Dharma Master again instructed her to single-mindedly recite his name. Having done so, she too—
He recovered. Whenever the Dharma Master treated or saved anyone, he never required the use of decoctions or medicine;

he simply instructed them to single-mindedly recite his name and to offer their wealth and goods as alms, whereupon their illnesses would be cured according to those actions—instances too numerous to record.

Later, there were times when those whose illnesses had been cured came to report it to him, and the Dharma Master accepted these offerings and redirected them as alms to beggars. Sometimes, while on the road, the Dharma Master...
Whenever he encountered a beggar whose clothes were tattered and worn, he would immediately take off his own garment and give it to them, departing instead clad in coarse clothing.

Furthermore, he was fond of releasing living beings; whenever he saw a household possessing nets or fishing gear, he would invariably take them and burn them. Upon seeing anyone selling living creatures, he would likewise act.
Regardless of their social rank, he would simply cast them into the water, after which he would have the sellers take their payment.
Later, at Fengjiang Village in Changshan County, he was walking alongside some fishermen. When they asked him for the fish in his basket to release them, the fishermen refused.
Instead, they lifted the basket and bathed it in the river. The Master then took the basket and threw it into the river; the fishermen were greatly incensed.
He beat him with his fists without restraint. The Dharma Master deeply reproached himself for his own fault. Later, at the Dongyang market, he saw fish intended for sale that he wished to release.
He encountered a man who was competing with him to buy them for his family's meal. The Dharma Master did not obtain the fish, so he said to the competitor:
"I fear that eating fish released for their lives will cause you abdominal pain. The man did not believe him; he took the fish back and gave them to his family to eat.

They all suffered excruciating pain in their hearts and bellies, and their conditions grew increasingly grave and critical. They immediately felt remorse and sought the Dharma Master to repent for their sins.
He went to their homes, and after a short while, they were all cured. Later, he went to the marketplace in Kuaiji to buy living creatures;
seeing two boats laden with fish, the Dharma Master covered them all in water and said to the fish-sellers, "This is the money for releasing these lives."
[He] said: "One should not take too much. The Dharma Master established the practice of releasing living beings and maintained it until his death without fail.

Whenever he traveled on the roads during heavy rain or snow, his robes remained unstained; they were exceptionally fragrant and pure. The Dharma Master cultivated his mind with diligent asceticism and traversed perilous and arduous terrain without ever feeling weary.
Consequently, he burned two of his fingers to serve as a lamp for the Dharma, making offerings to the Triple Gem.

Thereafter, he burned off six of his fingers as an offering to the Buddhas. While traveling, he came upon a narrow mountain stream where he encountered four boats carrying fish. He earnestly entreated them to purchase the fish so that they might be released;
however, as he had no goods to offer, he requested that they enter into a written contract. They went to Mount Qianbai to collect the payment, and he continued to accompany them along the way.
Along the way, he released captive animals. His clothing and provisions were nearly exhausted. On the thirteenth day of that month, he entered the Nunnery of Mount Ling at Shangmu Village in Qian.
He again burned two fingers; once the fingers were consumed, he proceeded to burn both arms.
Furthermore, someone came and earnestly requested the blood from the arm the Dharma Master had burned for use in treating an illness. The Dharma Master joyfully raised his arm.
He pricked his veins to give [blood] to them. On that same day, he again cauterized his old wound, and it blazed with brilliant light.
When his arm was completely consumed, he entered parinirvāṇa that very night. This was on the twenty-first day of the first month in the fourth year of the Tai-tong era;
he was forty-seven years of age. The monks jointly buried him at Yin-zhu in Qian. Previously, before the Dharma Master passed away, he had said to his disciples: "When I die..."
"Seven days hence, an auspicious sign shall appear. When the time arrived, the monastics and laypeople established a Great Unrestricted Assembly (*pañcavārṣika*).
At that moment, at the break of dawn, a divine light of five colors appeared, circling the temple pillars and lingering for a long time without dispersing.
Furthermore, a great radiance was emitted within the monastery for a full day and night; the entire assembly beheld it, and all gave rise to the bodhicitta.
Dharma Master Huìhé’s secular surname was Mǎ. He was originally a native of Màolíng in Fúfēng. His distant ancestors belonged to a family of hereditary scholar-officials.
During the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn dynasty, they followed the Five Princes southward to Lánlíng, where his descendants resided. When the Dharma Master was several years of age, he...
At that time, the entire family was away and he was alone in his private chamber when he suddenly saw a golden man with whom he played.
Thereafter, whenever he went out for excursions, the golden man would invariably accompany him in and out. When he reached the age of ten or so, he visited Xinghuang Temple;

Master Zhi saw him, circumambulated him three times, and remained in deep admiration and reverence for a long time. At the age of twenty, he received full ordination and resided at Jing’ai Temple. At that—
He examined and discussed the subtle, wondrous, and profound meanings of the sutras and vinaya, leaving nothing uninvestigated.

At that time, there was a Dharma Master named Yun, whose knowledge of the Dharma gates was vast and comprehensive, and whom both monastics and laity looked up to as their refuge. Upon meeting this Dharma Master, [the author] deeply admired him and constantly had him lecture on the texts in review.

In less than ten days, he fully understood the subtle purports within the sutras; even Master Yun himself came to look upon him with the realization that he could not surpass him. He was not yet thirty years of age.
Tenth: Having thoroughly investigated and understood the secret treasury of all Buddhas, his lectures and discussions were unrivaled.

At that time, there was also the Dharma Master Yin of Toudousi Temple, whose fame reached far and wide and to whom people from all quarters turned for refuge. Dharma Master Huihe then sold himself to provide offerings for him.

Bowing deeply, he consulted with Lord Yin, who said, "If you can chant the name of the Samādhi, the Śūraṅgama Dharma, in empty mountains, vast wildernesses, cities, and villages, its benefit will be profound and it will enable the accomplishment of all practices. The Dharma Master followed his advice;
every time after a lecture, he would invariably chant these words loudly at crossroads. At that time, there were some unruly disciples who would occasionally revile him.

He was subjected to beatings and flogging, yet the Dharma Master remained composed and unperturbed. When Lord Yin was about to pass away, the Master consulted him regarding his final affairs, asking, "Upon whom may I rely for guidance?
He replied, "Fu Dashi of Dongyang possesses innate wisdom and has a profound understanding of the Mahāyāna;
you may take him as your teacher and model. At that time, Dashi was in the capital, residing at Mount Jiang, where he was with Emperor Wu of Liang.
When Emperor Xiaozong established the orthodox teachings, the Dharma Master paid his respects and requested to become his disciple. Initially, he stayed at the residence of Upādhyāya Yan in Kuaiji.
Yan said, "I am a person of indolence; how could I possibly meet with the Reverend Dharma Master?

Thereupon, he refurbished his robes, bathed himself until pure, and led him into his room, where they remained in close fellowship for a long time. The Dharma Master then took his leave and traveled to Dongyang.
At that time, the disciples of Dongyang learned that the Dharma Master was about to arrive.
The layman Pumin went to the county seat to visit Shen Hou and said to him suddenly, "The Upādhyāya has taken a vow in the capital to become a disciple of the Mahāsattva;
he is now coming here specifically to make offerings. His teacher is arriving now. Upon hearing these words, Shen Hou raised his voice and scolded him, saying, "Pumin is arrogant and conceited!"
Although Emperor Gaozong repeatedly invited the Śrī, he could not be brought there. How much less would he have come from afar to see the Great Being (Mahāsattva) and listen to his teachings?
[The Master] universally took pity on him but did not answer. Eleven days later, the Śrī finally arrived. Emperor Gaozong immediately went to pay his respects and inquire after his well-being.
He asked, "Why have you suddenly come here? He replied, "I came specifically to pay my respects to the Great Being. Emperor Gaozong’s heart was greatly moved.
Feeling shame and remorse, he followed the ācārya into the mountains to pay his respects and organized a dāna assembly.

When the Mahāsattva saw that the Dharma Master had arrived, he rejoiced and praised him, preaching to him the path of unsurpassed bodhi. The Dharma Master accepted this teaching with deep devotion and made offerings, never shunning hardship or suffering.
In the first year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, the Dharma Master said to his disciple Faquan: "We must purchase [the necessary materials] immediately."

Although its essential nature is empty, it can bestow the principles of the Dharma. When observed, it has no form; when called upon, it has sound.

It serves as the great general of the Dharma, transmitting the scriptures through the precepts of the mind. Like the taste of salt in water or the presence of blue resin in lacquer, it is definitively existent, yet its form is not seen.

The mind-king is also like this: dwelling within the body, it enters and exits through the gate of the face; responding to objects and following circumstances, it is sovereign and unimpeded, accomplishing all that it does.
To fully realize the fundamental consciousness-mind is to see the Buddha in the consciousness-mind. This mind is the Buddha; this Buddha is the mind.

Although the nature of the mind is empty, the essence of greed and anger is real. By entering this Dharma-gate, one attains Buddhahood while sitting upright.
Having reached the other shore, one obtains the *pāramitās*. A true seeker of the Way observes their own mind; knowing that the Buddha is within, they do not seek him outwardly.

The mind is itself Buddha; Buddha is himself the mind. When the mind is clear, one recognizes Buddha; when one is fully enlightened, one recognizes the mind. Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from Buddha there is no mind.
That which is not Buddha is unfathomable; it is incapable of any function. Clinging to emptiness and lingering in quiescence, one drifts and sinks within this state.
